d: person who lives in seclusion and often in solitude
plain: person who lives alone in seclusion
ex: The monk spent three years of his life as a [[recluse]], praying and meditating.
mn: re + close — closes himself off from society, becomes a hermit.

plain: to prevent or head off in advance
ex: The government took steps to [[forestall]] an economic downturn by increasing government spending.
mn: Fore (before) + stall (stop) = to stop something before it happens.

ex: Despite the ceasefire, there have been [[sporadic]] outbreaks of violence between the warring factions.
mn: Sporadic is the opposite of periodic — periodic things happen regularly, sporadic things don't.

ex: People in an advanced stage of starvation often have [[distended]] bellies.
mn: Think 'distend' = 'stretch' — a distended stomach is stretched/swollen out.

ex: If humanity colonizes Mars, it will become a tabula rasa on which we will inscribe our [[immutable]] values and beliefs in a new environment.
mn: Mutation = change in genes. Im- (not) + mutable = cannot change.

ex: NASA announced that it would delay the launch of the manned spacecraft until the radiation from the solar flares [[abated]].
mn: Rhymes with 'rebate' (a price reduction) — abate = reduce.

ex: When addressing the nation, the president generally has an air of [[decorum]].
mn: Think 'decor' — keeping things decorous and proper for a formal occasion.

d: to argue over insignificant and irrelevant details
plain: to argue over trivial, unimportant details
ex: The lawyers spent so much time [[quibbling]] over details that they made little progress in reaching an agreement on the central issue.
mn: Hindi: 'kyun bill itna zyada hai?' — you nitpick and complain over small details on a bill.

ex: A compendium about the fascinating history of tea distilled everything into just twenty pages.
mn: A 'compact' medium — compendium packs a whole topic into a short summary.

ex: In recent years, many areas of China have been undergoing a [[metamorphosis]], transforming themselves from predominantly agricultural areas to industrial ones.
mn: Think of a caterpillar's literal metamorphosis into a butterfly — total transformation.

d: to vary; go in different directions from the same point
plain: to split apart in different directions
ex: The two economists' forecasts began to [[diverge]] sharply after the policy announcement.
mn: Two roads that 'diverge' in a yellow wood — they split and go different ways.

ex: Some research suggests that people with an [[abstemious]] lifestyle tend to live longer than people who indulge their appetites.
mn: Focus on 'abs' — to keep abs, you eat and drink carefully, in moderation.

d: something out of the proper time
plain: something placed in the wrong time period
ex: Some experts regard the retirement age of 65 as an [[anachronism]] at a time when people in the developed world have much longer life expectancies than previously.
mn: 'Chron' = time (chronometer). An- (not) + chron + ism = something not in its correct time.

plain: a claim or assertion put forward as true
ex: The professor's main [[contention]] was that the theory had never been properly tested.
mn: A contention is what you contend (argue) for — the claim at the center of a debate.

ex: President Abraham Lincoln displayed remarkable [[resolve]] in preventing the Confederate states from seceding.
mn: To 'resolve' to do something is to firmly decide — resolve as a noun is that firmness itself.

d: a piece of broken glass or pottery
plain: a broken fragment (of glass or pottery)
ex: Archeologists were able to reconstruct the drinking vessel from [[shards]] found around the ancient campsite.
mn: 'S + hard' — it's hard to piece broken shards of pottery back together.

ex: Bob apologized for his [[boorish]] behavior at the party, saying he hadn’t realized that it was such a formal occasion.
mn: Hindi 'boor' sounds like 'bura' (bad) — boorish behavior is bad-mannered and rude.

plain: a beginner, especially one just starting out
ex: The coach said that some of the team’s [[fledglings]] would play in Saturday’s game.
mn: A fledgling bird has just grown its flight feathers — a beginner just starting out.

ex: No one questioned the [[probity]] of the judge being considered for elevation to the U.S. Supreme Court; what was at issue was his controversial views on several important issues.
mn: 'Pro' + high standards — probity is unquestioned integrity and moral uprightness.

d: the state of having conflicting emotional attitudes.
ex: John felt some [[ambivalence]] about getting married before finishing college.
mn: Sounds like 'ambulance' — in an emergency you feel ambivalence: relief and fear mixed together.
trap: not simple indifference — means torn between two opposing feelings

ex: Innovation often requires challenges to orthodox thinking; for example, in the late 1960s, scientists from the U.S. Department of Defense’s Advanced Research Projects Agency presented their idea of a vast network of computers to leading scientists from IBM and AT&T—companies with innumerable research breakthroughs to their credit—and were [[derided]] as impractical visionaries.
mn: 'De-ride' — like riding a horse backward, people will ridicule you for it.

ex: The book argues that a new investigation into Marilyn Monroe’s death is [[warranted]] by new evidence released by the FBI under the Freedom of Information Act.
mn: A 'warrant' gives legal justification — something warranted is properly justified.

ex: Some biologists have theorized that our belief in our ability to act as [[autonomous]] agents is in conformity with the theory of evolution because it gives us a sense of meaning and purpose in our lives that helps us to survive.
mn: Auto- (self) + nomos (law/rule) — an autonomous region rules/governs itself.

ex: During the Cold War, the United States maintained a large number of nuclear weapons as a [[deterrent]] to aggression by the Soviet Union and its allies.
mn: Deter + rent — a high rent deters tenants from renting; it discourages the action.

ex: The task of writing a research paper is [[arduous]], but if it is broken down into logical steps it becomes less daunting.
mn: Read it as 'hard to do for us' — arduous tasks are strenuous and exhausting.

ex: Many scholars flourish in the [[rarefied]] intellectual atmosphere of the Institute for Advanced Studies in Princeton, New Jersey.
mn: Rare + field — an environment where the air (or company) is thin, refined, elite.
trap: not just 'rare' — connotes refined, elevated atmosphere

ex: The debate judge cautioned participants not to engage in [[invective]], but rather in reasoned and decorous discourse.
mn: In + vective (from 'vehere', to carry) — words carrying force and venom, verbal abuse.

ex: The chairman of the Federal Reserve used his testimony before Congress to [[disabuse]] his audience of the idea that the business cycle had been eliminated by the unprecedented period of prosperity.
mn: Dis- (remove) + abuse (misuse/misconception) — to free someone of a wrong idea.
trap: not related to 'abuse' — means to correct a false belief

plain: a person who thinks and acts independently
ex: Bernie Sanders of Vermont has a reputation as a [[maverick]]; he is one of only two members of the United States Congress who is independent (that is, not a member of the Republican or Democratic Party).
mn: A maverick cowboy rides his own way, breaking from the herd and convention.

plain: present but not yet developed or visible
ex: Some experts in human psychology believe that we are just beginning to explore the [[latent]] powers of the human mind.
mn: Re-spell as 'latent talent' — potential ability that's hidden, not yet developed.

ex: Many technological projects are interdisciplinary, requiring a knowledge of fields as [[disparate]] as physics and biology.
mn: Dis- (apart) + par (equal) — parts that are not equal or alike, fundamentally different.

ex: Investigators [[dismissed]] the man’s account of a visit to another planet aboard an alien spacecraft as the product of an overactive imagination.
mn: To 'dismiss' an idea is to wave it away, reject it from further thought.

ex: Heathcliff, the protagonist of Emily Bronte’s novel Wuthering Heights, feels great [[antipathy]] for Edgar Linton, the man who marries the woman he loves.
mn: Rhymes with and is the opposite of 'sympathy' — antipathy is strong dislike.

plain: a light, non-serious manner or tone
ex: The comedian has a gift for finding an element of [[levity]] in the most serious of subjects.
mn: Lev- (light, as in 'levitate') + ity — a light, unserious touch to something.

ex: The senator’s position keeps [[vacillating]] between remaining neutral and lending his support to the proposal.
mn: Sounds like 'oscillate' — swinging back and forth between two positions.

d: high praise, especially of a person who has recently died
plain: high praise, especially for the dead
ex: After the death of Abraham Lincoln, many [[eulogies]] of him appeared in newspapers throughout America.
mn: Eu- (good) + logos (words) — good words spoken about someone, often at a funeral.

d: one-sided; committed to a party, group, or cause; prejudiced
ex: Supporters of constitutional monarchy believe that while in this system, as it is generally practiced today, virtually all power is vested in popularly elected assemblies, the institution of the monarchy continues to serve a purpose as a focus of national unity above the furor of [[partisan]] politics.
mn: Parti- (party) + san — someone strongly loyal to one political party or side.

plain: one who habitually doubts accepted beliefs
ex: Like the nihilist, a comprehensive philosophic [[skeptic]] can be a difficult person to debate: if you tell him you know you exist, he is likely to ask you to prove it—and that can be harder than it first appears.
mn: Skeptic sounds like 'inspect-ic' — someone who inspects and doubts every claim.

plain: to extract the essential core of something
ex: In his book Men of Ideas: Some Creators of Contemporary Philosophy, Bryan Magee manages to [[distill]] the essence of leading thinkers such as W. V. Quine, John Searle, Iris Murdoch, and Noam Chomsky.
mn: Like distilling liquor — boiling something down to its purest, essential form.

d: to adorn; decorate; enhance; make more attractive by adding details
plain: to decorate or add details to make more attractive
ex: The story he had been told was so powerful that the writer felt no need to [[embellish]] it.
mn: Em- + BELL — hang a bell (ornament) on the tree to decorate it.
trap: can also mean to exaggerate/add fictitious details to a story

plain: a mismatch or lack of fit between things
ex: There is an [[incongruity]] between the poem’s solemn tone and its light-hearted theme.
mn: In- (not) + congruity (agreement) — things that don't fit or agree with each other.

ex: In sentencing the convicted man to a life sentence, the judge took into consideration the fact that he did not seem to be at all [[contrite]] about his crime.
mn: Con- (thoroughly) + trite (worn down) — worn down by guilt, thoroughly sorry.

ex: The jury had difficulty following the witnesses’ [[desultory]] testimony.
mn: A desultory approach jumps around at random and 'results' in nothing solid.

d: act of straying from the main point
plain: a temporary departure from the main topic
ex: The novel Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance by Robert M. Pirsig contains many fascinating [[digressions]] from the main story that discuss topics such as Platonic philosophy.
mn: A 'digression' literally means stepping (gress-) away (di-) from the main path.

d: to lessen another’s anger; to pacify
ex: After his team’s third consecutive winless season, the Big State football coach opened his address to the irate alumni with a barrage of clichés and euphemisms to try to [[placate]] them: “Gentlemen, it is not my intention today to pull the wool over your eyes. Heaven only knows I have given my all. I have truly made the old college try. Unfortunately, however, by any reasonable criteria we have been less than completely successful in our endeavors, but I assure you that hope springs eternal in the human breast and next year we will rise to the occasion, put our noses to the grindstone and emerge triumphant in the face of adversity. I certainly admit that we have had a run of bad luck but that is nothing that can’t be cured by true grit and determination.”
mn: PL + ac + ATE — offering someone a plate of food to satisfy and calm them.

plain: to draw out a response or reaction
ex: The Socratic method is designed to [[elicit]] responses that guide the student toward understanding.
mn: Opposite pairing: implicit (understood) / explicit (stated) — elicit = to draw out.

d: to replace, especially to displace as inferior or antiquated
plain: to replace something as outdated or inferior
ex: Malay was the lingua franca of the Malay peninsula for centuries, but in many parts of that region it is being [[superseded]] in that role by a European interloper, English.
mn: When a SUPER new version arrives, it supersedes (replaces) the obsolete old one.

plain: a stale, overused expression or idea
ex: Though Sarah’s marriage didn’t seem to be going well, she took comfort in the [[platitude]] that the first six months of a marriage were always the most difficult.
mn: A platitude is a 'flat' statement — flattened by overuse into a cliché.

ex: The Gettysburg Address is full of [[felicitous]] phrases such as “government of the people, by the people, and for the people.”
mn: Sounds like 'felicitation' — praised with well-chosen, fitting words.

ex: The [[salubrious]] effects of exercise on both physical and mental health have been well documented.
mn: Salu- as in 'salute to health' — salubrious air or climate is health-giving.

plain: to increase or improve in value or quality
ex: Although it is widely believed that the primary objective of the researchers developing the Internet was to secure the American nuclear missile system, in fact their main goal was to foster science by [[enhancing]] the ability of technology to disseminate information among scientists.
mn: En- (make) + hance (from 'enhauncer', raise) — to raise something's quality.

plain: impossible to please or appease; unyielding
ex: Once an [[implacable]] foe of capitalism, the People’s Republic of China in recent years seems, in practice if not in principle, to have embraced it.
mn: Sounds like 'unpleasable' — someone who can never be pleased or calmed down.

plain: deviating from what is normal or expected
ex: When a person’s behavior becomes [[aberrant]], his or her peers may become concerned that the individual is becoming a deviant.
mn: Ab- (away) + err (to stray) — straying away from the normal path, abnormal.

plain: pompous and overly elaborate in speech
ex: The orator abandoned [[grandiloquent]] phrases and instead uses simple and direct language.
mn: Grand + eloquent — an eloquent speaker delivering an overly grand, pompous speech.

plain: to satisfy fully, especially an appetite
ex: The bully [[satiated]] his fury by pummeling the helpless little boy.
mn: 'I sat and ate' till I was completely full and satisfied.

plain: to avoid telling the truth; be evasive
ex: Journalists accused government leaders of [[prevaricating]] about the progress of the war.
mn: Pre- (before) + var (truth) + icate (gate) — a gate placed before the truth, hiding it.

plain: to imitate in an attempt to equal or surpass
ex: The young pianist strove to [[emulate]] the technique of the great masters.
mn: Grandma gave me an 'amulet' so one day I could 'emulate' my hero.

ex: [[Implicit]] in the review is the idea that the writing of serious literature is a moral undertaking.
mn: Pairs with 'explicit' (clearly stated) — implicit is understood without being said.

plain: to speak of as unimportant; belittle
ex: Though sometimes [[disparaged]] as merely an intellectual game, philosophy provides us with a method for inquiring systematically into problems that arise in areas such as medicine, science, and technology.
mn: 'Display a rage' on someone — you belittle them by venting anger at them.

plain: excessively eager to please or obey
ex: Tom’s tendency to submit meekly to any bullying authority is so great that his wife suggested he overcome this [[obsequiousness]] by taking an assertiveness training course.
mn: Obsessed with saying 'qui' (yes in French) to everyone — overly submissive.

plain: an urgent situation demanding immediate action
ex: Astronauts must be prepared for [[exigencies]] such as damage to their spacecraft’s life support system.
mn: Exigency ~ exit + emergency — you remember the emergency exit only in a crisis.

ex: Many British writers recall with loathing the [[castigation]] they received at school.
mn: Think of harsh public censure — being 'cast out' and scolded severely.

ex: The technique of telling a story through a [[disjointed]] narrative is a technique best left to masters of the modern novel such as James Joyce and William Faulkner.
mn: Dis- + jointed — the joints (connections) between parts have come apart.

ex: According to psychologists, human beings are naturally [[wary]] of strangers.
mn: Sounds like 'worry' — you become wary (cautious) when you have things to worry about.

d: so high as to prevent the purchase or use of; preventing; forbidding
plain: so costly as to discourage purchase
ex: Most people in poor countries are unable to purchase a computer because of its [[prohibitive]] price.
mn: A prohibitive price effectively 'prohibits' you from buying it.

ex: “In friendship, as well as in love, the mind is often [[duped]] by the heart.” (Philip Dormer Stanhope)
mn: A 'duplicate' (fake) used to fool people — dupe = to trick.

ex: The senator launched into a [[tirade]] against the proposed budget cuts.
mn: Sounds like 'tired' — your mom gets tired after a long angry tirade.

ex: The judge [[admonished]] the jury to discount testimony that had been ruled inadmissible.
mn: A parent will admonish (gently scold/warn) a child for misbehaving.

d: to contradict; misrepresent; give a false impression
plain: to give a false impression; contradict
ex: The boxer’s childlike face [[belies]] the ferocity with which he can attack opponents in the ring.
mn: 'Belie' contains 'lie' — it gives a false, misleading impression.

ex: Most economists believe that the best way to prevent [[indigence]] is to expand employment opportunities.
mn: Owning only a cheap car (Indica) not a luxury one (Opel Astra) — a sign of indigence.

ex: The theologian discussed the question of why a [[beneficent]] and omnipotent God allows bad things to happen to good people.
mn: Bene- (good) + fic (do) — one who does good, kindly deeds.

ex: The idea of equality and liberty [[diffused]] through society after the French Revolution.
mn: Dif- (apart) + fuse (pour) — pouring outward and spreading in all directions.

ex: The songwriter says that it is easy to [[inadvertently]] use the melody of another song when composing.
mn: In- (not) + advertently (paying attention) — done without paying attention, by accident.

ex: [[Apathy]] was high in the election because there was no major controversy or issue to arouse voter interest.
mn: A- (without) + pathos (feeling) — without feeling, indifferent. Weaker than 'antipathy' (dislike).

plain: difficult to understand; known to few
ex: Many classical and biblical references known to educated nineteenth-century readers are now considered [[recondite]] by most readers.
mn: 'Re-conduct' — the professor had to re-teach the obscure topic since students didn't get it.

plain: causing or tending to cause sleep
ex: For some people the best [[soporific]] is reading a boring book.
mn: Hindi: after eating too many 'soo puri', you feel sleepy — soporific induces sleep.

plain: showing off learning; fussy about minor details
ex: The Sophists have acquired a reputation as being learned but rather [[pedantic]] entertainers who gave didactic talks on every subject under the Sun; the truth, however, is that some of the Sophist philosophers (notably Protagoras) were very able thinkers.
mn: Sounds like 'pandit' (scholar) — obsessed with bookish, technical detail.

ex: Since the early 1950s, government planners have faced a dilemma: Spend a great deal of money to keep cities [[viable]] by rebuilding decrepit infrastructure, or allow them to decay.
mn: Think 'survivable' — a viable plan is one that can actually survive/work.

ex: The [[assiduous]] intern double-checked every figure before submitting the report.
mn: 'Ass in the dust' — a donkey working hard, diligently, in the dirt.

d: the act of assuming to be true or real
ex: Science proceeds on the [[supposition]] that knowledge is possible.
mn: Sup- (under) + position — the position/premise placed under an argument, an assumption.

d: full of holes; permeable to liquids
plain: full of tiny holes; letting liquid through
ex: If you go camping, make sure to spend enough money to buy a tent with a roof that is not [[porous]].
mn: A porous rock has visible 'pores' (holes) that let liquid pass through.

ex: The school provides extensive support and guidance for [[neophyte]] teachers.
mn: 'Neo' (new, like Neo from The Matrix) + phyte — a new fighter, a beginner.

plain: lasting only a very short time
ex: The cherry blossoms are prized in part because their beauty is so [[ephemeral]].
mn: Sounds like 'e-funeral' — an electronic thing that's gone fast, short-lived.

plain: a person of low moral character
ex: The social worker refused to give up hope of reforming the criminal who was generally regarded as a [[reprobate]].
mn: Rep- (repeatedly) + rob + ate — someone who repeatedly robs, showing no morals.

ex: The autobiography tells the story of the billionaire’s journey from [[penury]] to riches beyond his imagining.
mn: Pen + rupee — not even a rupee left to buy a pen, extreme poverty.

plain: able to be passed through; penetrable
ex: Wetsuits, used by divers in cold water, are [[permeable]] to water but designed to retain body heat.
mn: Per- (through) + meable (able to pass) — able to be passed through.

ex: Farmers in the arid areas called for the government to build a dam to provide water to irrigate their crops and provide hydroelectric power; however, this plan was opposed by environmentalists, who dislike [[inundation]] of land because it would have an adverse effect on wildlife.
mn: Nun + date — asking a nun on a date would get you flooded with angry letters.

ex: The monk lived an [[austere]] life, with nothing but a bed, a table, and a single candle.
mn: Think of a stark, unadorned monastic life — austere, no comforts, no frills.

ex: The [[aggregate]] wealth of a country includes private as well as public resources and possessions.
mn: A + GRE + gate — everyone's total GRE score combined to reach the university gate.

ex: The duty the judge considers most [[onerous]] is sentencing convicted criminals.
mn: Sounds like 'onus' — when something is on us, it feels like a heavy burden.

d: free of cunning or deceit; artless
ex: One of the charms of the novel is that the [[guileless]] hero manages to defeat the scheming villain.
mn: Guile (cunning/trickery) + less (without) — literally, without cunning.

d: to support with proof or evidence
plain: to support with facts or evidence
ex: The validity of fossil identification is [[substantiated]] by data from geology and carbon-14 dating.
mn: 'Substance' + -ate — to give substance (solid backing) to a claim with evidence.

ex: Many people in the west are [[reticent]] to criticize science, which in the view of many has become a sacred cow.
mn: Stereotype of a quiet saint/monk — reticent to speak or draw attention.

d: the act of estimation by projecting known information
plain: a prediction based on known data
ex: The economist’s [[extrapolation]] suggests that the economy will grow by 4% next year.
mn: Like TV channels predicting election results based on early known trends.

ex: The German army commander Erwin Rommel was known as the “Desert Fox” as a result of his [[audacious]] surprise attacks on Allied forces in World War II.
mn: Audi- (to hear, as in 'audible') — to be heard by millions, you must be bold and daring.

d: to combine into a unified whole
plain: to combine into a single unified whole
ex: In early 1999, six municipalities were [[amalgamated]] into an enlarged city of Toronto, Canada.
mn: A + mal(e) + game + mate — combining/uniting together with your teammate as one unit.

plain: a noticeable difference between two things
ex: The book studies the [[discrepancy]] in values and outlook between men who fought in the war, whether voluntarily or not, and those who remained civilians.
mn: Dis- + creep + fancy — a 'creepy' thing and a 'fancy' thing don't match; a discrepancy.

d: use of agreeable or inoffensive language in place of unpleasant or offensive language
plain: a mild word substituted for a harsh one
ex: An illustration of the tendency toward [[euphemism]] is the change (reflecting the political concerns of the day) in the accepted appellation of poor countries from the unambiguous poor, to undeveloped, to underdeveloped, to less developed, to develop ing.
mn: 'Pass away' instead of 'die' — a euphemism softens unpleasant truth into gentler words.

ex: The assessment of some skeptical critics of existentialism is that it is generally a view of life created by a group of thinkers whose distinguishing characteristic is that they are [[morose]].
mn: Hindi: 'mor ro raha hai' (peacock is crying) — sorrowful, sullen, morose mood.

d: impossible to penetrate; incapable of being affected
ex: We were amazed how Laura could sit at the noisy party studying organic chemistry, [[impervious]] to the noise around her.
mn: Im- (not) + 'pravesh' (Hindi: entry) — cannot be entered or affected.

d: composed of identical parts; uniform in composition
plain: uniform throughout; made of identical parts
ex: The committee was surprisingly [[homogeneous]] in both background and opinion.
mn: Homo- (same) + genos (kind) — made of all the same kind of parts.

ex: The country’s leader found that the people became more [[tractable]] when he made them believe there was a great threat facing them that only he could overcome.
mn: Sounds like 'tractor' — a tractor makes a field easy to manage and control.

d: to approach; come together; tend to meet
plain: to move toward meeting at a point
ex: Although the People’s Republic of China and India are rivals in many ways, in certain areas their interests [[converge]].
mn: Co- (together) + verge (edge) — edges coming together to meet at one point.

d: to retract a statement or opinion
plain: to formally withdraw a previous statement
ex: The bishop told the theologian that he must [[recant]] his heretical teaching or risk excommunication.
mn: Re- (again) + cant — 'I told you again and again, it's rejected' — to retract a claim.

plain: a mark of shame or disgrace
ex: A problem with giving formal psychological treatment to a child who is believed to be poorly adjusted to society is that he may acquire a [[stigma]] as a result of officially being labeled as deviant, and he may act to corroborate society’s expectation.
mn: Imagine a shocking, disgraceful act — it leaves a permanent stigma (mark of shame).

d: to dishonor; disgrace; cause to be doubted
plain: to damage someone's reputation or credibility
ex: The candidate’s attempt to [[discredit]] his opponent by spreading damaging rumors about him failed.
mn: Dis- (not) + credit — to take away someone's credibility/reputation.

ex: Alcohol has been shown to seriously [[impair]] the functioning of the brain.
mn: Opposite of 'repair' — while repair mends, impair damages/injures.

plain: the ability to produce a desired effect
ex: A cardinal rule of medicine is that the [[efficacy]] of a treatment should be measured against the seriousness of its side effects.
mn: Check if your AC has the 'efficacy' (efficiency) to actually cool the room.

ex: Buddha counseled that one should try to remain [[imperturbable]] through life’s vicissitudes.
mn: Im- + perturb (disturb) + able — not able to be disturbed, unshakably calm.

d: to swagger; display to impress others
plain: to walk with a proud, showy gait
ex: The star quarterback [[strutted]] around campus the entire week after he led his team to a 42-0 win over the county’s top-ranked team.
mn: Picture someone walking with chest out, head high, showing off — strutting.

plain: to become less intense; calm down
ex: Army personnel told the civilians to wait for the violence to [[subside]] before reentering the town.
mn: Hindi: police telling a violent mob 'sub side ho' (everyone move aside/settle) — to subside.

d: marked with thin, narrow grooves or channels
plain: marked with parallel grooves or lines
ex: The [[striated]] surface suggested to the geologist that he was walking over an area in which there once had been a torrent of water.
mn: Think of 'striped' rock surfaces — thin parallel grooves cut by water or ice.

ex: The psychology researcher’s experiment postulates that the brain is [[analogous]] to a digital computer.
mn: Remember it from 'analogy' — an analogous case is one comparable to another.

ex: Because it deals with death and grieving, the funeral business has produced a [[plethora]] of euphemisms such as “slumber room” for the place where the corpse is placed for viewing.
mn: Hindi: mother insisting 'ple le, thoda aur le' (eat more) until there's a plethora of food.

ex: The [[laconic]] actor seemed to be a good choice to play the strong, silent hero in the western.
mn: 'LAC' = lack — a lack of words; the laconic person speaks very little.

d: superficial; not thorough; performed really as a duty
plain: done without care or interest, as a routine duty
ex: The [[perfunctory]] inspection of the airplane failed to reveal structural faults in the wing.
mn: Doing someone else's ('paraya') work carelessly, just as a routine duty — perfunctory.

ex: Fred’s [[resolution]] to succeed is unshaken despite the many setbacks he has suffered.
mn: Sounds like 'revolution' — America's resolution/determination to win independence.

ex: The speaker launched into a [[diatribe]] against what he called “the evils of technology.”
mn: A diatribe is a fierce verbal 'attack' — bitter criticism delivered at length.

ex: In the Hindu epic poem the Bhagavad-Gita, Lord Krishna warns the hero, who is reluctant to fight, that refusing to fight would be a [[craven]] act.
mn: Craven is simply the opposite of 'brave' — a coward.

ex: An argument sometimes advanced for euthanasia is that the amount of money spent on prolonging a person’s life for several months is exorbitant in relation to the [[paucity]] of funds available for preventive health programs and child health, both of which are highly cost-effective.
mn: Only one 'paav' (bread) available for the whole city — extreme scarcity.

ex: In these days of credit card and installment plan buying, [[frugality]] seems to have become a rarely practiced virtue.
mn: Free + girl — getting something for free avoids wasting money, hence frugal/thrifty.
trap: not negative like 'stingy' — frugality is a virtue, careful with money

ex: The comedian’s [[facetious]] comments about prominent politicians kept the audience amused.
mn: Face + not serious — a facetious remark is made with a not-serious, joking face.

plain: something that triggers a change or event
ex: The oil crisis acted as a [[catalyst]] for the country's shift toward renewable energy.
mn: In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without itself being consumed.

ex: The football coach was pleased to see the team get to work on the task of improving its tackling skills with [[alacrity]].
mn: Linked to 'creativity' — creative people tackle tasks with eager enthusiasm.

d: to affirm; declare to be true
ex: The witness continued to [[aver]] that she had never left the building that night.
mn: 'A very' confident statement — aver means to state something with full confidence.

d: produce and release substance into organism
plain: to produce and release a substance
ex: The pancreas gland [[secretes]] a fluid that helps fat, carbohydrates, and protein to be digested in the small intestine.
mn: Related to 'secret' — a gland secretes (releases) fluid, though not literally hidden.

ex: The student could not understand why no one took seriously his [[fatuous]] comments.
mn: Sounds like 'fat-headed' — a smug, foolishly self-satisfied person.

ex: [[Perennial]] warfare has left most of the people of the country in poverty.
mn: Like a perennial river that flows year-round — long-lasting and persistent.

ex: Everyone but an astrophysicist seems to be [[confounded]] by the question, “What happened before the Big Bang?”
mn: 'Con-fusion found' — confound sounds like finding total confusion.

ex: Sue has a [[penchant]] for science, while her brother is more interested in the arts.
mn: P + enchant — something that enchants you becomes a strong liking, a penchant.

d: division into two usually contradictory parts
plain: a division into two contrasting parts
ex: The philosopher is a dualist who argues that there is a [[dichotomy]] between the mind and physical phenomena.
mn: Di- (two) + cut — cutting something into two contrasting parts, a dichotomy.

ex: The governor ordered an audit to investigate alleged financial [[chicanery.]]
mn: Sounds like 'shikari' (Hindi: hunter) — using cunning tricks to trap prey.

ex: The leader of the country made [[conciliatory]] statements assuring the world that his country did not intend to acquire nuclear weapons.
mn: Sounds like 'consoling' — soothing words meant to calm hostility.

ex: When a person starts a sentence, “I don’t mean to appear [[disingenuous]],” one might be tempted to suspect that the person is being just that.
mn: Opposite of 'ingenuous' (genuine, naive) — disingenuous means insincere, crafty.
trap: means insincere/crafty, not simply 'not clever' or 'not ingenious'

d: based on a false idea or fact; misleading
plain: based on a mistaken belief; misleading
ex: The belief of the Nazis that they could create a “master race” was based on the [[fallacious]] premise that some races are inherently superior to others.
mn: Focus on 'fallac-' which looks like 'false' — based on a false premise.

plain: only slightly related to the main subject
ex: The judge ruled that the evidence had only a [[tangential]] bearing on the case and directed the lawyer to present only a brief summary of it.
mn: From geometry: a tangent line only barely touches a circle — a peripheral connection.

plain: to limit or be sparing with something
ex: [[Stinting]] on funding for education strikes many people as shortsighted.
mn: A 'stint' of something is a limited, rationed amount — to stint is to be sparing.

d: band of colors produced when sunlight passes through a prism; a broad range of related ideas or objects
plain: a broad, continuous range of related things
ex: The political science course deals with the whole [[spectrum]] of political ideologies.
mn: Like the color spectrum from a prism — a full continuous range of variety.

plain: open to more than one interpretation
ex: The gender of the Mahayana Buddhist deity Avalokitesuara, the god of infinite mercy, is [[ambiguous]] in both China and Japan, where the god is sometimes called a goddess.
mn: Ambi- (both) + guous (like 'guess') — you're left guessing between two meanings.

ex: One of the primary uses of solar cells is in spacecraft to provide electric power; this is because space is an environment uniquely suited to these devices since it has no weather to [[occlude]] the Sun and it is not susceptible to interruptions in sunlight caused by the rotation of the Earth.
mn: Rhymes with 'exclude' — to occlude is to shut/block, keeping something out.

ex: Betty warned her husband that he must stop his [[prodigal]] spending on sports cars and expensive clothing.
mn: Think of the 'prodigal son' who wastefully squandered his inheritance.
trap: the antonym of frugal, not 'talented' (a common confusion with 'prodigy')

plain: liable to change suddenly and unpredictably
ex: Currency traders complained that the exchange rate had become dangerously [[volatile]].
mn: Like volatile computer memory (RAM) — erased/changed the instant power is cut.

ex: The newspaper reporter looked for [[disinterested]] witnesses to the events so that she could get an objective account of what had happened.
mn: Dis- (apart from) + interest — standing apart from any personal stake, hence unbiased.
trap: not 'uninterested' (bored) — disinterested means impartial, no personal stake

d: record of a voyage; record of daily activities
plain: a written record of events or activities
ex: Although no longer required to do so by the Federal Communications Commission, many amateur radio operators nevertheless keep a meticulous record of stations they communicate with, [[logging]] the details of each contact.
mn: A ship's log is a written record kept of each day's voyage and events.

plain: quickly and easily provoked to anger
ex: The [[irascible]] old man complains every time someone makes a little noise.
mn: Focus on 'rasc-' as in 'rascal' — a hot-tempered, easily irritated troublemaker.

ex: The writer’s recollection of her childhood is [[saturated]] with sunshine and laughter.
mn: To saturate is to soak something completely, leaving no room for more.

ex: Study of the historical evidence has shown that there is only a [[tenuous]] connection between the country Plato describes in The Republic and the legendary land of Atlantis.
mn: Sounds like 'tenuous' ~ 'thin as tennis players' — a thin, weak connection.

d: having many twists and turns; highly complex
plain: full of twists and turns; excessively complex
ex: Only the world’s leading mathematicians are able to follow the [[tortuous]] line of reasoning used by the English mathematician Andrew Wiles to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem via the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture.
mn: A tortoise never moves in a straight line — its path twists and turns, complex.
trap: not the same as 'torturous' (painful) — tortuous means winding/complex

ex: A recent anthropological theory is that human beings are [[gregarious]] creatures that are comfortable living in groups of around 150 individuals.
mn: From 'aggregate' (gather together) — a gregarious person loves gathering in groups.

ex: The monk kept an [[ascetic]] cell with nothing but a mat and a bowl.
mn: Someone who gives up all 'aesthetics'/comforts — an ascetic, living austerely.

ex: Behind the professor’s [[stolid]] appearance is a fun-loving, gregarious character.
mn: Sounds like 'solid' — solid against tears/emotion, unmoved and impassive.

d: capable of being shaped by pounding; impressionable
ex: Gold is prized by jewelers for being so [[malleable]] that it can be hammered into thin sheets.
mn: Sounds like 'meltable' — a malleable metal can be reshaped, like something meltable.

d: absence of government; state of disorder
ex: The American philosopher Robert Nozick does not advocate [[anarchy]]; rather, he argues for the merits of a minimal state that would not violate the natural rights of individuals.
mn: An- (without) + archy (rule) — without any ruling government, chaos.

plain: not harmful; not likely to cause offense
ex: The bodyguard looked [[innocuous]] enough, but under his jacket were several weapons that could kill an attacker in seconds.
mn: In- (not) + nocuous (noxious) — literally, not harmful.

plain: a mournful poem or song, often for the dead
ex: The poet wrote an [[elegy]] for his old friend, filled with quiet grief.
mn: 'E-legy' sounds like a song for a 'legendary' person who has died — a lament.

d: to enjoy; have a distinctive flavor or smell
plain: to enjoy fully, taking one's time
ex: The coach gave his team a day off practice to [[savor]] their big victory.
mn: Savor rhymes with 'flavor' — you savor (taste and enjoy) the flavor of food.

ex: Many historians have criticized British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain for trying to [[appease]] Adolf Hitler in the 1930s.
mn: App + peace — to appeal for peace, calming someone by giving in to demands.
trap: in modern GRE usage often carries a negative connotation (giving in unwisely)

d: to specify as an essential condition
plain: to specify as a required condition
ex: The president’s lawyer [[stipulated]] that he would appear before the investigative committee, but would answer only questions directly relevant to the issue at hand.
mn: Staple + it — you staple documents to guarantee/stipulate they stay together.

ex: The [[ebullient]] candidate for president appeared before his supporters to announce that he had won in a landslide.
mn: Getting a new Enfield Bullet makes you 'e-bullet-ent' — bursting with excitement.

plain: to stir up or incite trouble
ex: The government accused the newspaper of [[fomenting]] unrest in the country.
mn: Like foam forming when you stir hot soapy water — to foment is to stir up unrest.

plain: to ease pain or soothe emotion
ex: A warm meal did much to [[assuage]] the refugees' hunger and fear.
mn: Sounds like 'a-swage' (as in swagger dying down) — to soothe pain or hunger.

plain: to calm or pacify someone upset
ex: The prime minister tried to [[mollify]] people protesting the tax increase with a promise that she would order a study of other means to raise revenue.
mn: Sounds soft like 'mellow' — to mollify is to make someone mellow and calm again.

ex: People sometimes confound psychology and psychiatry: the former is the science that studies cognitive and affective functions, both normal and [[pathological]], in human beings and other animals, whereas the latter is a branch of medicine that deals with mental disorders.
mn: Path- (disease, as in pathology) — a pathological condition departs from normal health.

ex: The bank’s hermetically sealed vault has kept the manuscript in [[pristine]] condition for 50 years.
mn: Sounds like 'priestine' — as pure and untouched as something kept by a priest.

plain: the planned route of a journey
ex: We planned our [[itinerary]] to be flexible, so that if we especially enjoyed a particular place we could stay there longer.
mn: An itinerary is the planned route/schedule for your trip — think trip 'i-tinerary'.

ex: Neo-Platonism—an [[eclectic]] third-century synthesis of Platonic, Pythagorean, Aristotelian, Stoic, and Jewish philosophy—was an essentially mystical belief that a person can achieve spiritual emancipation through union of the soul with the ultimate source of existence.
mn: Sounds like 'elect' — to elect (choose) the best bits from many different sources.

ex: The principal warned the student that his [[truculence]] might one day land him in jail.
mn: A truck driver who recklessly hurt someone provokes the aggressive fury of villagers.

ex: The expert in English believes that since the tendency to use hyperbole is natural and often enriches the language, it should not be [[proscribed]].
mn: You PREscribe (subscribe to) a magazine; you PROscribe (ban) one you want stopped.

plain: to partially relieve pain or difficulty
ex: According to some commentators, one of the weaknesses of capitalism is that, although it is very efficient at increasing absolute wealth, it is not as successful at [[alleviating]] relative poverty; thus, a person living in a slum in America may be reasonably well off by historical standards, but he might perceive himself to be poor compared to members of the bourgeoisie, whom he sees regularly buying luxury goods that he is not able to afford.
mn: All the 'evil' (pain) is eaten up, leaving you relieved and eased.

d: hard to understand; known only to a few
plain: understood by only a small, specialized group
ex: The footnotes were full of [[esoteric]] references that only a specialist could decode.
mn: Like specialized 'historic' knowledge known only to a few experts.

plain: to leave suddenly and secretly, often to escape trouble
ex: A warrant is out for the arrest of a person believed to have [[absconded]] with three million dollars.
mn: Ab- + scond — you 'absent' yourself in a second, fleeing and hiding secretly.

ex: Nadine Cohodas’s biography of the blues singer Dinah Washington keeps the reader [[apprised]] of the racism black Americans had to endure.
mn: Whoever informs you well 'deserves a prize' — apprise means to inform.

ex: During the Cold War, there was a [[tacit]] assumption on the part of both the Soviet Union and the United States that neither side would launch an unprovoked nuclear attack against the other side.
mn: Sounds like 'take it' — permission given silently through action, not words.

ex: The nurse is extremely [[solicitous]] of the health of every patient in the ward.
mn: To solicit (ask earnestly) implies you're anxiously, attentively concerned about the outcome.

plain: a puzzling problem with no clear solution
ex: The paradoxical statement “This statement is false” presents us with a [[conundrum]].
mn: Hindi riddle: 'drum ke andar kaun hai?' — a classic unanswerable conundrum.

ex: Ironically, the book about how to write lively, engaging prose is an [[insipid]] piece of writing.
mn: In- (not) + sip + id — a drink you wouldn't even want to sip, lacking flavor.

plain: to reduce in force or intensity; weaken
ex: Modern digital radio equipment allows even signals that have been greatly [[attenuated]] to be transmitted by one station and received by another station.
mn: 'Tenu' (you) + ate less — the less you eat, the more attenuated (thinner/weaker) you get.

d: unsure of how to act; weak
ex: The president admonished Congress, saying that although it faced difficult choices it must not be [[irresolute]].
mn: Ir- (not) + resolute — lacking the firmness to make a resolution/decision.

ex: There is an adage in philosophy that everyone is born either a Platonist or an 2 Aristotelian, meaning that everyone has a predisposition to believing either that reality is completely “here and now,” or that there exists a more [[profound]], hidden reality.
mn: What true 'professionals' find through research is profound, deep knowledge.

ex: Eighty meters is a portion of the radio spectrum where a shortwave listener can often hear [[loquacious]] “hams” chatting (“chewing the rag” in amateur radio parlance) for hours.
mn: From root 'loqui' meaning 'to speak' — loquacious means overly fond of speaking.

ex: If you read his speech carefully you will see that the senator is [[insinuating]] that his party has taken the wrong path.
mn: Trying to hint/imply something to someone without stating it outright — insinuate.

plain: a state of weariness and lack of energy
ex: After the death of his wife, Steven suffered a three-month period of [[lassitude]] and depression.
mn: Drinking a heavy lassi after lunch leaves you drowsy, weary, and lethargic.

plain: asserting opinions as facts without proof
ex: Since every case is unique, jurists must not be [[dogmatic]] in applying precedents to make their decision, but instead must base their decision on a combination of such precedents and the facts of the case at hand.
mn: Read backward, dogmatic hints at 'I am god' — someone rigidly certain they're always right.

plain: not able to be passed through
ex: The virus protection software is said to be [[impermeable]] to attacks by malicious software sent over the Internet.
mn: Im- (not) + permeable — the opposite of permeable, cannot be passed through.

d: overly polite; willing to please; obliging
ex: Although France and Germany have a close relationship, neither would consider the other a [[complaisant]] ally.
mn: Com- + plais (please) — overly eager to please and agree with others.

ex: The American tradition of the tall tale uses [[hyperbole]] to depict a world in which the inhabitants and their deeds are larger than life, as befitting a people inhabiting a vast landscape.
mn: Hyper- (beyond) + bole (speak) — speaking beyond the literal truth, exaggerating.

ex: The lawyer presented a [[cogent]] argument that left the jury with little doubt.
mn: A gentle (cogent) but firm argument is the one that actually convinces people.

ex: It is difficult to imagine the [[opprobrium]] heaped on a person who is a traitor to his or her group.
mn: Sounds like 'opium' — using a banned drug brings public shame and disgrace.

ex: The biologist Loren Eisely had what could be described as a [[reverent]] attitude toward nature.
mn: People bathe reverently at a river's end as an act of worship and deep respect.

plain: a slow, mournful song, often for the dead
ex: The music critic described the movement of the symphony portraying the hero’s last days as “ [[dirge]] like.”
mn: 'Dirge' starts like 'die' — a mournful song sung to honor someone who died.

d: idol worship; blind or excessive devotion
plain: excessive devotion to someone or something
ex: During the Protestant Reformation images in churches were felt to be a form of [[idolatry]] and were banned and destroyed.
mn: Idol + adulation combined — excessive, worshipful devotion to an idol or person.

plain: temporarily inactive but capable of activity
ex: There is a considerable body of evidence showing that many diseases, such as ulcers, asthma, and hypertension have a large psychological component; the working hypothesis is that they represent manifestations of [[dormant]] emotional disturbances.
mn: DORM as in dormitory (sleep) — a dormant volcano is 'sleeping', inactive for now.

plain: to polish until shiny; improve one's reputation
ex: The poet T. S. Eliot [[burnished]] his reputation as one of the master poets of the twentieth century with Four Quartets, four long poems published between 1936 and 1942.
mn: Related to 'varnish' — used to polish and shine up wood or a reputation.

ex: The columnist’s [[caustic]] comments on government policy did not win her any friends among government officials.
mn: Caustic soda burns on contact — caustic remarks 'burn' with biting sarcasm.

ex: As a result of the strength of his opposition to the Vietnam War Senator Eugene McCarthy overcame his [[diffidence]] and ran against President Lyndon Johnson for the Democratic nomination for president.
mn: Simply the opposite of 'confidence' — diffidence is shy self-doubt.

plain: extremely careful and precise about details
ex: Science is an empirical field of study based on the belief that the laws of nature can best be discovered by [[meticulous]] observation and experimentation.
mn: Sounds like 'matriculation' — you must be meticulous (careful) to pass tough exams.

d: showy; trying to attract attention; pretentious
plain: showy and meant to attract attention
ex: A member of the bourgeoisie might purchase a vacation home on Maui or Cape Cod that some would regard as an [[ostentatious]] display of wealth, but that the person regards as simply a pleasant place to go on vacation.
mn: Sounds like 'stunt-atious' — performing showy stunts just to attract attention.

ex: The idea of the universe originating at a certain point in time seems [[problematic]] to many scientists.
mn: A problematic issue is one that literally 'poses a problem' still unresolved.

d: seeming to be logical and sound, but not really so
plain: seems true but is actually false
ex: The article systematically rebuts the [[specious]] argument advanced by the so-called expert in the field.
mn: Sounds like 'suspicious' — but specious means an argument that LOOKS right yet is actually false.
trap: not 'suspicious'; means deceptively plausible, not doubtful

ex: The establishment of the state of Israel from Palestinian territory in 1948 was the realization of a hallowed dream for Zionists, but for many Palestinians it meant the [[sanctioning]] of continued domination of their land by Europeans.
mn: Officially give the OK — 'SANCTION' an action means to approve it.
trap: as a noun, 'sanction' can also mean a penalty — opposite sense

plain: an introductory statement before the main text
ex: Along with the opening words of the Declaration of Independence and the Gettysburg Address, the [[preamble]] to the Constitution of the United States contains some of the most memorable language in American history.
mn: PRE (before) + AMBLE (walk): the 'walk before' the main text begins.

plain: to weaken or lose energy gradually
ex: Noticing that the students’ attention was [[flagging]], the professor gave them a short break.
mn: Like a flag drooping with no wind — losing energy or vigor over time.
trap: verb sense (to droop/tire), not the noun 'flag' (banner)

ex: The novel describes the main character as “being of an [[indeterminate]] age, somewhere between 50 and 60.”
mn: IN + DETERMINE + ATE: not able to be pinned down exactly.

ex: In her essay the student had the [[effrontery]] to argue that school is largely a waste of time.
mn: He has the FRONT to argue rudely — shameless boldness.

plain: to openly disregard or defy a rule
ex: In his book Poetic Meter and Poetic Form the distinguished literary critic Paul Fussel discusses the dangers poets face when they [[flout]] poetic conventions.
mn: FLOUT sounds like 'foul' — a player who fouls openly defies the rules.
trap: not 'flaunt' (show off); flout means to defy/disregard

d: strong or sharp in smell or taste; penetrating; caustic; to the point
plain: sharply strong in smell, taste, or wit
ex: Slang frequently expresses an idea succinctly and [[pungently]].
mn: Think of pungent chili — a sharp smell/taste that stings; pungent wit stings too.

plain: something that comes before; a forerunner
ex: The [[precursor]] to the theory of plate tectonics was the theory of continental drift.
mn: PRE (before) + CURSOR (pointer) — something that points the way in advance.

d: to wallow or roll; toss about; be in turmoil
plain: to wallow or toss about in confusion
ex: The pigs [[weltered]] about happily in the mud.
mn: Pigs WELTER (roll) happily in mud — wallowing in turmoil.

ex: The dry desert air caused the bodies of the dead animals to [[desiccate]] quickly.
mn: Think of a DESICCANT packet (like in shoe boxes) — it dries everything out completely.

plain: a perfect model or example of excellence
ex: The epic poet Homer was regarded by the ancient Greeks as a [[paragon]] of literary excellence.
mn: The Paragon brand markets its shoes as models of perfection — a paragon is the perfect example.

d: to cause to happen; throw down from a height
plain: to cause something to happen suddenly
ex: Full-scale American entry into World War II remained unpopular with the vast majority of Americans until a declaration of war was [[precipitated]] by the Japanese attack on the naval base at Pearl Harbor, a day that President Roosevelt predicted, in a memorable phrase, would “live in infamy.”
mn: Like rain PRECIPITATING suddenly — to precipitate is to make something happen abruptly.
trap: as adjective, 'precipitate' means hasty/rash — a related but distinct sense

plain: hardened or accustomed to something unpleasant
ex: After 20 years in the army, the chaplain had not become [[inured]] to the sight of men dying in the battlefield.
mn: IN + URE (like 'endure') — you endure something so long you grow used to it.

ex: There was a movement to condemn slavery among some of the writers of the Declaration of Independence, but despite many misgivings, the proposal was dropped in [[deference]] to the objections of a number of people.
mn: If there's no DIFFERENCE worth fighting over, you show deference and yield to the other's wishes.
trap: implies yielding one's own judgment, not just plain 'respect'

ex: Samuel Johnson gave this [[sage]], albeit hard, advice to writers wishing to improve their style: “Read over your compositions, and whenever you meet with a passage that you think is particularly fine, strike it out.”
mn: Related to 'saga' — the wise elder whose legendary advice is retold as a saga.
trap: as a noun, sage is also a wise person or an herb

ex: The literary critic [[lauded]] Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, calling it a novel that “explores the tension between a person’s life as a social being and his or her individual consciousness.”
mn: LAUD sounds like 'loud' applause — praising someone loudly.

ex: The new policy is likely to [[engender]] resentment among longtime employees.
mn: Two genders coming together ENGENDER (produce/give rise to) a child.

ex: Quantum theory led to the formulation of the uncertainty principle, which was [[delineated]] in 1937 by Werner Heisenberg.
mn: DE-LINE-ATE: draw a clear LINE around something — outline it precisely.

d: condition of being able to be shaped or formed; pliability
plain: the ability to be shaped or molded
ex: The sociologist is continually amazed by the [[plasticity]] of social institutions.
mn: Like PLASTIC, which can be molded into new shapes — plasticity is shapeability.

plain: pompous, using grand but empty language
ex: Nearly lost in the senator’s long, [[bombastic]] speech were several sensible ideas.
mn: BOMBS make a big, empty noise to impress people — bombastic speech is loud and hollow.

plain: based on observation or experiment, not theory
ex: Some people erroneously cite the theory of relativity as support for ethical relativism, whereas in reality the former is a scientific theory, while the latter is a moral issue, and thus by its nature is not subject to [[empirical]] verification.
mn: EMPIRICAL sounds like 'experiment' — knowledge gained from testing, not theorizing.
trap: not 'imperial'; unrelated word, means evidence-based

ex: The Internet—together with the availability of relatively inexpensive personal computers—has greatly [[facilitated]] the ability of ordinary people to conveniently exchange information with one another and with large computer systems.
mn: FACIL- as in 'facile' (easy) — to facilitate is to make something easy.

d: perceptive; exhibiting keen insight and good judgment
plain: showing keen insight and good judgment
ex: [[Discerning]] movie critics have praised the work of producer Stanley Kubrick, who produced such excellent films as 2001,
mn: Read it as 'di-screening' — someone who screens everything twice, very observant and alert.
trap: GRE sense close to 'discriminating' (fine judgment), not 'picky'

ex: The Congressional Medal of Honor is the highest [[approbation]] an American soldier can receive.
mn: Ap + PROBATION: you get formal APPROVAL/confirmation after your probation period.
trap: not 'probation' (a punishment period); means approval

ex: The prime minister’s [[precarious]] hold on power ended when she lost a vote of confidence in Parliament.
mn: PRE + CARE + IOUS: you must take extra CARE because the situation is risky/precarious.

d: to take possession for one’s own use; confiscate
plain: to seize or take for one's own use
ex: The government moved to [[appropriate]] private land for the new highway.
mn: As a verb (stress on the last syllable), to APPROPRIATE is to take something for oneself.
trap: verb sense (seize) differs sharply from the common adjective sense (suitable)

ex: The salesperson said he would [[rescind]] his offer to sell the goods at a 10% discount unless he received full payment within 24 hours.
mn: RESCIND sounds like 'resign' — but rescind cancels an agreement rather than a job.

ex: The novel tells the story of the hero’s [[perfidious]] lover.
mn: PER + FID (fidelity, i.e. loyalty) + OUS — perfidious is the opposite of loyal.

ex: An argument against welfare is that it encourages people to be [[indolent]].
mn: IN + DOLENT, like Hindi 'dolna' (to move) — indolent means not moving, i.e. lazy.

d: notice ordering someone to appear in court
plain: a legal order to appear in court
ex: The judge issued a [[subpoena]] for the man but the prosecutor had little hope that he would appear because he was living abroad.
mn: Sounds like 'saboot post karna' in court — a subpoena orders you to appear with evidence.

ex: Her [[artless]] honesty charmed everyone at the dinner, though it occasionally embarrassed her hosts.
mn: Without the ART of deception — plain, guileless honesty.
trap: not 'unskilled'; means guileless/without deceit

d: a person possessing expert knowledge or training; a person of informed and discriminating taste
plain: an expert with refined judgment or taste
ex: The art [[connoisseur]] selected works by Van Gogh, Rembrandt, and Picasso for the exhibition.
mn: Sounds like Hindi 'kaun inse sure nahi hoga' — no one is more sure/expert than a connoisseur.

ex: The maple syrup is so [[viscous]] we had trouble pouring it.
mn: VISCOUS relates to 'viscosity' — honey has high viscosity, thick and sticky.

d: to tear out; scoop out; overcharge
plain: to overcharge, or to scoop/tear out
ex: The store is able to [[gouge]] its customers because it is the only store in the area that carries that particular line of merchandise.
mn: Buying pricey branded 'gouges' (slang for goggles) — you feel the shopkeeper is gouging you.

ex: The linguist and political commentator Noam Chomsky has been described as gleefully [[iconoclastic]] because of the zeal with which he attacks many of the central beliefs of American society.
mn: ICON (idol) + CLASH — one who smashes idols/traditions into pieces.

plain: inactive; unable or unwilling to move
ex: The teacher was frustrated by his inability to get an answer to his question from his [[inert]] class.
mn: Recall chemistry: INERT gases barely react — inert means lacking the ability to move or act.

ex: In his book, Chronicles, Bob Dylan describes the process of how some of his songs went from an [[inchoate]] state to finished, well-produced songs.
mn: INCHOATE sounds like 'in chaos' — still a formless, early-stage jumble.
trap: not 'chaotic' forever; means just starting to take shape

ex: The officer had no choice but to recommend that the [[recalcitrant]] soldier be court-martialed.
mn: Like calcite, a hard mineral that resists breaking — a recalcitrant person resists control.

ex: The judge ruled the testimony inadmissible because he considered it [[mendacious]].
mn: MENDACIOUS sounds like 'mend' — you mend (cover up) the truth by lying.

ex: Each side in the negotiations accused the other of [[intransigence]], so talks broke down.
mn: IN + TRANSIGENT (from 'transact/transition') — refusing to budge or transition at all.

plain: to win over or appease someone
ex: M.E.W. Sherwood, an author alive at the time of the U.S. Civil War, eloquently expressed the sacrifice made by soldiers on both sides of that great conflict: “But for four years there was a contagion of nobility in the land, and the best blood of North and South poured itself out a libation to [[propitiate]] the deities of Truth and Justice. The great sin of slavery was washed out, but at what a cost!”
mn: PROF + PITY — if you want the professor's pity, you must appease/propitiate them.

ex: Their [[garrulous]] uncle dominated every family dinner with rambling stories.
mn: Think 'garrulous chatter' — words tumbling out nonstop, like a gargling rattle with no rules.

d: to reject as having no authority
plain: to reject as having no authority
ex: In the 1960s, many black leaders such as Malcolm X and Stokely Carmichael [[repudiated]] integration and nonviolence in favor of black separatism and passive resistance in the fight for civil rights.
mn: He ate the pudding, then tried to REPUDIATE (deny) eating it.

plain: to prove something false with evidence
ex: The eighteenth-century English author Samuel Johnson claimed to have [[refuted]] the philosophy of idealism by kicking a large stone.
mn: RE + FUTE (like 'confute') — to refute is to disprove with evidence, not just disagree.
trap: not simply 'deny/disagree'; implies proving false with evidence

ex: The drug morphine—considered by doctors to be one of the most effective analgesics—is the principal [[derivative]] of opium, which is the juice in the unripe seed pods of the opium poppy.
mn: DERIVE + -ATIVE — something derived from an original source, often lacking originality.
trap: as adj. also means 'unoriginal/imitative' in criticism

plain: to make a bad situation worse
ex: The release of carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels has increased the amount of this gas in the atmosphere, [[exacerbating]] the naturally occurring “ greenhouse effect” that has predominated in Earth’s recent past.
mn: Latin 'acerb-' means bitter/harsh — to exacerbate is to make more bitter, to worsen.

ex: It is a plausible hypothesis that the atheistic and materialistic philosophy of Marxism was readily accepted in China because of its similarities with Confucian views on spiritual matters, which had a [[pervasive]] influence in China for many centuries.
mn: PERVASIVE relates to 'pervade' — it spreads through and permeates everything.

ex: In the United States, malpractice suits have raised the cost of medicine because doctors must pay more for insurance, and thus increase their fees [[commensurately]].
mn: COM (together) + MENSURATE (measure) — measured together, i.e. proportional to.

ex: There is a natural [[propensity]] to stress the importance of what one is saying by exaggerating it.
mn: A PRO-pensity is a strong, built-in PRO-leaning toward doing something.

plain: to strip away or deprive of
ex: The candidate for secretary of defense pledged to [[divest]] himself of the shares he held in defense-related companies.
mn: Opposite of INVEST: DI + VEST (an inner garment) — divest is to strip it off.

ex: The soldiers’ poor treatment of the prisoners [[negated]] any goodwill they had built up among the population.
mn: NE (no) + GATE (door) — there's no entrance through that door; it's nullified.

ex: Judges are expected to conduct themselves with [[propriety]], especially in the courtroom.
mn: PROPR- sounds like 'proper' — propriety is behaving properly and correctly.

plain: to overlook or tacitly accept wrongdoing
ex: The coach refused to [[condone]] the players' unsportsmanlike conduct.
mn: CON + DONE — treating a wrong as already 'done and over,' tacitly letting it pass.
trap: means to overlook/tacitly permit, not to actively approve

ex: Frederick Copleston, author of the nine-volume History of Philosophy, was undoubtedly one of the most [[erudite]] people who ever lived.
mn: ERUDITE sounds like 'e-read-ite' — one who has read widely and deeply.

plain: to clear from blame or guilt
ex: The report [[exculpated]] the FBI of any wrongdoing in its handling of the investigation.
mn: EXCULPATE sounds like 'ex-culprit' — no longer a culprit, cleared of the charges.

ex: Coach Knight is [[obdurate]] about one thing: the offensive line is the heart of his football team.
mn: OB + DURATE (like 'durable') — hard and durable in one's position, unyielding.

plain: giving off light; bright and clear
ex: The Moon is the most [[luminous]] object in the night sky.
mn: LUMIN- as in 'illuminate' — full of light, glowing.

ex: [[Gullible]] members of the audience believed the young performer’s claim that he had composed “Hey, Jude.”
mn: GULLIBLE sounds like 'gull' — a seagull snatches any food offered, easily fooled.

ex: After the 18-hour flight from New York to Singapore, the passengers were [[lethargic]].
mn: LETHARGIC sounds like being 'allergic' to activity — low energy, sluggish.

ex: The conman could not bring himself to take advantage of the [[ingenuous]] boy.
mn: IN + GENUINE — someone genuinely naive and trusting, without guile.
trap: not 'ingenious' (clever); a classic sound-alike confusion

ex: A good judge must hold his or her judgment in [[abeyance]] until all the facts in a case have been presented.
mn: A + BEYANCE sounds like 'buoyancy' — held suspended above the ground, not yet resolved.

d: to consign to an inferior position
plain: to assign to a lower rank or position
ex: After the scandal, the once-star player was [[relegated]] to the reserve team.
mn: Your relatives cry at the GATE because you RELEGATE them there instead of letting them in.

d: stubborn; unmanageable; resisting ordinary methods of treatment
plain: stubbornly resistant to control or treatment
ex: The general practitioner called in specialists to help determine the cause of the patient’s [[refractory]] illness.
mn: REFRACTORY sounds like 'refuses to react' to normal control or treatment — stubborn.
trap: in medicine specifically means resistant to treatment

plain: relating to beauty or artistic taste
ex: Members of the English [[aesthetic]] movement, such as Oscar Wilde, were proponents of the doctrine of art for art’s sake, which is the belief that art cannot and should not be useful for any purpose other than that of creating beauty.
mn: AES + THETIC — think of it as the opposite of 'pathetic': concerned with beauty.

ex: “ [[Phlegmatic]] natures can be inspired to enthusiasm only by being made into fanatics.” (Friedrich Nietzsche)
mn: When we hoist a FLAG, the automatic reaction is calm and unexcited — phlegmatic.

ex: Many children appreciate Dr. Seuss’ [[whimsical]] stories.
mn: WHIMSICAL sounds like 'whim' — driven by playful, unpredictable whims.

plain: to belittle or criticize someone's reputation
ex: According to a recent biography of Napoleon Bonaparte, the famous leader felt a need to [[denigrate]] women.
mn: From Latin 'nigr-' (black) — to denigrate is figuratively to 'blacken' someone's name.

ex: Do not let the difficulty of learning the 800 words in Essential Words for the GRE [[daunt]] you.
mn: DAUNT sounds like 'haunt' — a haunted house frightens and discourages you from entering.

plain: to make a bad situation better
ex: Knowing they could not stop the spread of a contagion in a few days, health authorities worked to inhibit its spread and to [[ameliorate]] its effects by issuing warnings to the public and initiating immunization programs.
mn: Imli (tamarind) AMELIORATEs the taste of bland food — it makes things better.

d: concluding part of a literary or musical composition; something that summarizes or concludes
plain: the concluding part that wraps things up
ex: The [[coda]] of the Danish composer Per Norgard’s Sixth Symphony seems to return to the serene sounds of the opening.
mn: CODA is the final section in a piece of music — the concluding part.

d: act of trespassing or violating a law or rule
plain: an act that violates a law or rule
ex: The teacher made it clear on the first day of the term that she would not countenance any [[transgression]] of classroom rules.
mn: TRANS (across) + AGGRESSION — crossing a border aggressively, violating the rule.

plain: to slow down or block progress
ex: The development of the western region of China has been [[impeded]] by a lack of trained workers.
mn: From 'impedance' in electronics — resistance that impedes the flow.

plain: extremely complex and hard to follow
ex: Unraveling the [[convoluted]] genetic code is one of the great achievements of modern science.
mn: Like a mathematical CONVOLUTION — twisted and folded, hard to follow.

ex: The psychologist discounted the [[anomalous]] behavior of the soldier, saying it was merely a short-term effect of the stress of battle.
mn: ANOMALOUS relates directly to 'anomaly' — an abnormal deviation.

plain: native to and common in a particular area
ex: Malaria, once [[endemic]] to the area, has now been largely eradicated.
mn: Unlike an EPIDEMIC (spreads widely), an ENDEMIC disease stays confined to one region.
trap: not the same as 'epidemic'; endemic means confined to a region

ex: The businessperson has earned a reputation as someone who never [[equivocates]] and can be trusted to do exactly what he promises.
mn: EQUI (equal) + VOCAL (sound) — making sounds so similar the meaning stays unclear.

ex: With the pervasive influence of American culture, “fast-food” restaurants are [[proliferating]] in many countries.
mn: PRO + LIFE-erate — like life multiplying rapidly, cells proliferating.

ex: The witness’ testimony appeared to be [[veracious]] at first, but under cross-examination, several inconsistencies appeared.
mn: Root 'VER' means true, as in veracious (truthful) and verisimilitude (appearance of truth).
trap: not 'voracious' (greedy/hungry); a classic sound-alike trap

plain: excessively eager to give unwanted help
ex: Some of us on the tour found the guide [[officious]], but others thought she was helpful and courteous.
mn: Picture a government OFFICE where clerks poke their nose into everyone's business.
trap: not 'official'; means annoyingly meddlesome, not authorized

ex: In Indian philosophy a position between monism at one extreme and dualism at the other is [[qualified]] nondualism, a philosophy in which reality is considered to have attributes of both dualism and monism.
mn: Primary sense: above standard. GRE sense (opposite!): limited/hedged, as in 'qualified support.'
trap: GRE sense = limited/hedged, opposite of the common sense (competent)

d: one who feigns illness to escape duty
plain: one who feigns illness to avoid duty
ex: The sergeant suspected the soldier was a [[malingerer]] trying to avoid combat duty.
mn: A child 'lingers' (MA-linger) near mom to avoid going to school — faking sickness.

ex: After World War II, the increased speed of industrialization and the [[burgeoning]] world population resulted in such an increase in pollution that it began to be recognized by some people as a threat to the human habitat, Earth.
mn: BURGEON sounds like 'bulge' — growing big and fast.

ex: To some non-philosophers, the discipline seems frivolous and [[futile]] because it produces no tangible benefits.
mn: FUTILE is not FERTILE — it produces nothing, unlike fertile ground.

plain: to disguise one's true feelings or motives
ex: “Miss,” the prosecutor said, “I believe you are [[dissembling]]. I want you to tell me the whole truth about what happened that night.”
mn: DIS + (re)SEMBLE — you make yourself resemble something you're not, hiding your true self.
trap: not 'disassemble' (take apart); means to feign/hide true motives

ex: In normal individuals, blood begins to [[coagulate]] about 20 seconds after a wound is sustained, thus preventing further bleeding.
mn: Think of the thick paste in a tube of Colgate — coagulate means to thicken.

ex: The senator showed his [[magnanimity]] when he conceded defeat to his opponent in the disputed election, saying that further uncertainty would be harmful to public confidence in the political system.
mn: Hindi 'Nani Ma' (grandmother) is always MAGNANIMOUS and generous with love and gifts.

d: to make unnecessary; to anticipate and prevent
plain: to make unnecessary by anticipating and preventing
ex: An experienced physician can often discern if a patient’s symptoms are psychosomatic, thus [[obviating]] the need for expensive medical tests.
mn: OB + VIA (way, like 'deviate') — clear something out of the way so it's no longer needed.

plain: to deny or dispute a claim
ex: No one can [[gainsay]] the fact that she put great effort into the project.
mn: She has GAINed weight but won't SAY it — she gainsays (denies) the fact.

plain: readily yielding to demands or rules
ex: The young negotiator is trying to learn the skill of being open to proposals by the other side without seeming too [[compliant]].
mn: One who never COMPLAINs and always obeys is COMPLIANT.

ex: The speaker in Andrew Marvell’s poem “To His Coy Mistress” [[reproaches]] his beloved for ignoring the passing of time and for not being willing to physically express her love for him.
mn: RE (again) + PROACH (approach) — you make someone approach again and again to answer for their fault.

ex: American soldiers were welcomed back to the United States with [[fervor]] after the end of World War II.
mn: Like exam FEVER — an intense, burning eagerness to study all night.

plain: overly bold or rude without right to be
ex: The new employee did not offer her advice to her boss because she was afraid he might consider it [[presumptuous]] for a recent graduate to make a suggestion to someone with 30 years experience in the field.
mn: Focus on 'PRESUME' — to overstep boundaries by boldly presuming or assuming.

d: introduce something into another thing already in existence; combine
plain: to combine or include as a part
ex: According to Bob Dylan in his autobiography, Chronicles, he systematically tried to [[incorporate]] what he learned about life and music into the songs he wrote.
mn: IN + CORPORATE (body) — to bring something into the body/whole; combine.

ex: The writer has a gift for making even the most [[banal]] observation seem important and original.
mn: BANAL rhymes with 'canal' — the same predictable, unoriginal route every single day.

d: to provide with written evidence to support
plain: to support with written evidence or records
ex: The insurance company asked Debbie to [[document]] her claim with letters from the doctors who treated her for her condition.
mn: As a verb, to DOCUMENT something is to back it up with documents/records.

plain: to fail to fulfill an obligation, especially a debt
ex: Economists have pointed out the danger of using government money to help banks in danger of [[defaulting]] on a loan: such help might encourage banks to take excessive risks on the future, knowing they will be “bailed out” by the government.
mn: Just as a DEFAULT setting kicks in when you fail to choose, to default is to fail an obligation.
trap: GRE sense is failing to fulfill an obligation, not just a 'preset option'

ex: The building was [[imploded]] in order to make way for the construction of a new apartment complex.
mn: EX-plode bursts OUT; IM-plode bursts IN — implode means to collapse inward.

d: an embankment that prevents a river from overflowing
plain: an embankment built to prevent flooding
ex: An extensive system of [[levees]] is the only way to prevent the river from flooding the area during periods of heavy rain.
mn: LEVEE sounds like 'level' — we level and reinforce the land so water can't seep through.
trap: not 'levy' (a tax or to impose); different word, same sound

ex: The cult of romantic love was a major factor in making a marriage for love, rather than for more [[pragmatic]] reasons, a ubiquitous phenomenon in the West by the nineteenth century.
mn: PRAGMATIC is close to 'practical' — both stress real-world usefulness over theory.

ex: Like the physicist, the abstract artist strives to identify the [[discrete]] elements of reality and to understand how they interact.
mn: Like discrete math, which deals with separate, countable values — discrete means distinctly separate.
trap: not 'discreet' (careful/tactful); classic homophone trap

plain: clearly expressed and easy to understand
ex: The eminent surgeon Dr. Christian Barnard, who performed the first human heart-transplant operation in 1967, made his views on euthanasia clear in this [[lucid]] injunction: “The prime goal is to alleviate suffering, and not to prolong life. And if your treatment does not alleviate suffering, but only prolongs life, that treatment should be stopped.”
mn: When you LOOK at someone's ID clearly, you understand them — lucid means clearly understandable.

ex: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux was a medieval French monk revered for his [[piety]].
mn: When you finally get PIE and TEA after being hungry, you thank god with devotion.

plain: a person who dislikes humanity in general
ex: One of the most famous [[misanthropes]] in literature is the protagonist of the seventeenth century French writer Moliere’s play Le Misanthrope (The Misanthrope).
mn: Greek 'misein' (to hate) + 'anthropos' (mankind) — one who hates mankind.

ex: During World War II Russian commanders counted on the bitter cold to [[enervate]] German soldiers invading their country.
mn: When you waste your ENERGY (e-NERV-ate), you become weak.
trap: not 'energize'; deceptively looks similar but means the opposite

ex: The [[insularity]] of many tribes in New Guinea allows anthropologists to study cultures that have been relatively uninfluenced by the modern world.
