mn: We INSULATE electrical wires to ISOLATE them from the environment — insularity is that isolation.

d: firmly established by nature or habit
plain: existing as a natural, essential part
ex: Some studies of random numbers generated by computers suggest that an [[inherent]] order exists in nature, since certain patterns appear that one would not expect in a random system, but skeptics dismiss such patterns as either artifacts of imperfectly designed experiments, or as the attempt of the human mind to impose a pattern where there is no intrinsic order.
mn: Like a trait passed down through HEREDITY — a habit that is naturally inherent.

ex: In a pluralistic society there exists a cacophony of [[discordant]] voices, each shouting to be heard.
mn: Focus on 'DISCO' — discos are always loud and inharmonious, just like discordant sounds.

plain: calmness and composure, especially under stress
ex: Emergency room doctors and nurses are trained to maintain their [[equanimity]] when treating patients.
mn: EQU (equal) + ANIMUS (spirit) — keeping an even, balanced mind under pressure.

ex: Although malignant tumors may remain [[quiescent]] for a period of time, they never become benign.
mn: QUIESCENT relates to 'quiet' — still and motionless for now.

plain: to swing or move back and forth
ex: The teacher [[oscillates]] between a student-centered approach to teaching and a subject-centered approach.
mn: Like an oscillating fan — OSCILLATE means to swing back and forth.

plain: to regard with great respect or reverence
ex: Mother Theresa is [[venerated]] for her compassion for the poor people of India.
mn: When you RATE someone very highly, you treat them with respect — venerate them.

ex: The boss has a reputation for hiring [[fawning]] employees.
mn: Like a crazy FAN who always flatters and courts favor to stay close to their idol.

d: to give a boost to; prop up; support
ex: The president has visited the state several times to [[bolster]] his sagging popularity there.
mn: Relate it to a BOLT — used to reinforce and support a structure.

ex: The judge sat, [[impassive]], listening to the man’s emotional account of the crime.
mn: 'I'm PASSIVE (not active)' — impassive means showing no feelings or emotion.

ex: The gas is intended to render enemy soldiers [[insensible]].
mn: IN + SENSIBLE — literally without sense/senses, i.e. unconscious or unaware.
trap: not the opposite of 'sensible' (wise); GRE sense is unconscious/unaware

plain: to support or reinforce, as an argument
ex: Some critics of the American legal system argue that the requirement of proving guilt “beyond a reasonable doubt” is too difficult a criterion to use, and [[buttress]] their case by citing the fact that objective studies suggest that only a very small number of criminals are successfully prosecuted.
mn: A BUTTRESS is a structure that props up a wall — to buttress is to reinforce.

ex: The skillful editor cut 20% of the words from the [[verbose]] manuscript without appreciably altering its meaning.
mn: VER(bal) + BOSE (boss) — imagine your boss being excessively verbal, talking on and on.

ex: The football team sat silently listening to their coach’s half-time [[harangue]] about poor tackling, dropped passes, and lost opportunities to score.
mn: When you're ANGry with HAR (her), she's subjected to a long angry harangue.

plain: to prod or provoke someone into action
ex: [[Goaded]] by his friends into trying out for the football team as a walk-on, Jeff went on to become an all-American linebacker.
mn: GOAD tells you to 'GO And Do it' — prodding someone into action.

ex: While belief in reincarnation appeared as doctrine first in India and was [[disseminated]] throughout Asia by Buddhism, it is interesting that it was accepted by the most influential philosophy of the West, Platonism, and by some important early Christian thinkers, such as the theologian Origen.
mn: DIS + SEMINATE, like a seminar — scattering ideas the way people scatter from a seminar.

ex: After returning home from his coast-to-coast trip, the truck driver sank into a peaceful [[torpor]], watching TV and dozing.
mn: The opposite of being a 'topper' — torpor is a state of dull, diligence-free sluggishness.

ex: General practitioners are equipped to deal with most psychosomatic disorders, but in [[intractable]] cases a psychiatrist is consulted.
mn: Things which cannot be brought onto the right TRACK — the opposite of tractable.

plain: a breaking apart or ending; also debauchery
ex: Some philosophers maintain that the [[dissolution]] of the body does not mean the destruction of the mind.
mn: The opposite of a RESOLUTION (a promise made) is a DISSOLUTION (a promise broken).
trap: can also mean moral dissipation/debauchery, not just 'breaking up'

d: to cause to become less harsh, severe, or painful; alleviate
plain: to make less severe or harsh
ex: Although the Supreme Court under the leadership of Chief Justice Warren Burger did not rescind any of the fundamental rulings of the Warren Court that preceded it, its decisions did [[mitigate]] the effects of some of the rulings of the Warren Court.
mn: Cover something unpleasant with dirt (mitti) to lessen its intensity — mitigate.

plain: lack of harmony or agreement; conflict
ex: In psychology, the term “cognitive [[dissonance]]” refers to a conflict resulting from inconsistency between one’s beliefs and one’s actions. For example, a soldier who believes that all killing is immoral but is forced to kill by his superiors might experience cognitive dissonance.
mn: DIS + SONANCE — the opposite of resonance; not in harmony.

d: one who is fanatically devoted to a cause
plain: a person fanatically devoted to a cause
ex: The Crusades of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries were conceived of by Christian [[zealots]] as a way to drive the Islamic interlopers from the Holy Land.
mn: ZEAL + LOT — someone who shows an extreme lot of zeal for their cause.

d: worldly as opposed to spiritual; concerned with the ordinary
ex: Paying bills and doing laundry are among the [[mundane]] tasks of adult life.
mn: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... the same MUNDANE routine every day.

ex: The meeting of the two women seemed [[inconsequential]] at the time, but in retrospect it led to one of literature’s great collaborations.
mn: 'Consequence' means result — inconsequential things have no result worth worrying about.

plain: to make impure by adding an inferior substance
ex: The unscrupulous company sells an [[adulterated]] version of the drug, and doesn’t inform consumers that they are getting a less efficacious drug than they think they are getting.
mn: They 'DULL THE' quality/rate of a product by adding cheap substitutes — adulterate.
trap: not related to 'adultery'; means to make impure by adding inferior ingredients

ex: The rule of law is regarded by many historians as one of humanity’s great achievements because since its inception citizens are no longer subject to [[capricious]] decisions and penalties of rulers.
mn: The PRICE of CARs keeps swinging unpredictably — capricious.

plain: to fall or drop suddenly and steeply
ex: The fighter jet, struck by an enemy missile, [[plummeted]] to earth.
mn: PLUMMET rhymes with 'comet' — a comet plummets sharply through the sky.

plain: likely to cause argument or controversy
ex: When genetic engineering began in the 1970s, there was a [[contentious]], and sometimes acrimonious, debate among scientists themselves about its dangers.
mn: A serious CONTENDER who takes competition too seriously always ends up quarreling.

plain: preparing wisely for future needs; frugal
ex: Most people have heard the story of the prodigal grasshopper and the [[provident]] ant that spends the summer saving food for the winter.
mn: PRO + VIDE (see ahead, like 'provide') — one who foresees needs and saves for them.
trap: not just 'kind'; implies foresight and frugality

ex: Considering that there are approximately 925,000 species of insects (more than all other species combined), [[entomology]] is a vast field of study.
mn: Easily confused with ETYMOLOGY (word origins) — ENTOMOLOGY studies insects (think 'ento' = bug-like).
trap: commonly confused with 'etymology' (study of word origins)

plain: relevant or fitting to the situation
ex: [[Apropos]] of nothing, the speaker declared that the purpose of life is to love.
mn: From French 'à propos' (to the purpose) — fitting and relevant to what's discussed.

ex: When considering what occupation to pursue it is prudent to consider [[intangible]] rewards as well as financial ones.
mn: IN + TANGIBLE (touchable) — cannot be touched; not physical, abstract.

plain: the current prevailing fashion or trend
ex: Although protectionist policies are not in [[vogue]] today, great capitalist democracies, such as Great Britain and the United States, flourished for long periods of their histories under protectionist trade policies that were nearly mercantilist—policies that imposed high tariffs on many foreign goods to promote domestic production.
mn: Think of Vogue magazine, the epitome of current fashion and trend.

d: branch of philosophy that examines the nature of knowledge
plain: the branch of philosophy studying knowledge
ex: A major question in [[epistemology]] is whether the mind can ever gain objective knowledge, limited as it is by its narrow range of sense experience.
mn: EPISTEME (Greek for knowledge) + -OLOGY (study of) — the study of knowledge itself.

plain: not able to be defended or maintained
ex: Skeptics are inclined to regard arguments for God’s existence from design as meaningless, since they rely on a logically [[untenable]] position that assumes the conclusion of their argument—God’s existence.
mn: UN + TENABLE (from 'tenere,' to hold) — a position that cannot be held.

ex: The new federal prosecutor promised voters that he would [[extirpate]] corruption in the state.
mn: EX (out) + STIRP (root, Latin) — to rip something out by the root, destroying it fully.

plain: a servile flatterer who caters to the powerful
ex: The boss had no respect for the employee because he considered him a [[toady]] who would do anything he said.
mn: A TOAD-y crouches low and grovels, just like a servile flatterer.

ex: Despite being an abridged edition of the 20-volume Oxford English Dictionary, the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary consists of two [[tomes]] that define over half a million words.
mn: TOME rhymes with 'home' — a huge scholarly volume heavy enough to be furniture.

ex: Two writers often mentioned as having an admirably [[pellucid]] style are Bertrand Russell and George Orwell.
mn: PEL + LUCID (clear) — clear as clear can be, both visually and in meaning.

d: careful in observing rules of behavior or ceremony.
plain: very careful about details and rules
ex: The prime minister reminded his staff that they must be [[punctilious]] in following protocol during the visit by the foreign head of state.
mn: PUNCTILIOUS relates to 'punctual' and 'punctum' (point) — precise about every single point.

d: sudden feeling of faintness or nausea; uneasy feeling about the rightness of actions
plain: a nagging doubt about the rightness of an action
ex: The judge had no [[qualms]] about sentencing the thief to five years imprisonment.
mn: QUALM sounds like a disturbed 'calm' — a small doubt that unsettles your conscience.

plain: to damage someone's reputation with false statements
ex: The ancient Greek philosopher Socrates was [[defamed]] as a teacher who corrupted the morals of his students.
mn: DE + FAME — to strip someone of their good fame or reputation.

plain: curved outward, like the outside of a sphere
ex: The term for a lens with one [[convex]] and one concave side is “convex-concave.”
mn: A CONVEX mirror bulges outward toward you — the opposite of concave, which caves in.
trap: opposite of concave; easy to mix up which way each curves

d: pertaining to riotous or drunken festivity; pertaining to revelry.
ex: For some people New Year’s Eve is an occasion for [[bacchanalian]] revelry.
mn: From BACCHUS, the Roman god of wine — bacchanalian means wild drinking and partying.

d: contemplating one’s own thoughts and feelings
plain: examining one's own thoughts and feelings
ex: In many ways William Wordsworth’s great poem The Prelude is an [[introspective]] work, retrospectively exploring his thoughts and feelings as he matured.
mn: INTRO (inward) + SPECT (look) — looking inward at your own mind.

plain: formed by volcanic heat or fire
ex: The presence of [[igneous]] rocks on the beach suggests that there was a volcanic eruption in the area millions of years ago.
mn: From Latin 'ignis' (fire), as in 'ignite' — igneous rock is formed by fire.

ex: After the battle all that could be heard was the [[plaintive]] cries of women who had lost their husbands.
mn: PLAINTIVE sounds like 'complain' — a sad, complaining tone.

d: fluent in an insincere way; offhand
ex: Sharon’s parents were not satisfied by her [[glib]] explanation of why she had not been able to study for the exam.
mn: GLIB rhymes with 'fib' — a glib talker fibs smoothly and effortlessly.
trap: not simply 'articulate'; implies insincerity or superficiality

plain: excessively ornate in style, or flushed red
ex: As he grew older, the novelist eschewed the [[florid]], ostentatious style of his youth in favor of a more direct and sparse style.
mn: From 'flora' (flower) — an overly flowery style, or a face flushed like a red flower.
trap: has two senses: ornate writing style AND ruddy complexion

d: to show plainly; be an indication of
plain: to clearly show or reveal a quality
ex: The student’s response to the teacher’s question [[evinced]] his ignorance of the subject.
mn: EVINCE sounds like 'evidence' — you evince (show evidence of) a feeling or trait.
trap: not 'evict' or 'convince'; means to plainly display/reveal

ex: Geoffrey Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales is the story of a group of Christian pilgrims who entertain one another with stories, ranging from the holy to the [[bawdy,]] on their journey to Canterbury Cathedral.
mn: BAWDY sounds like crude 'body' humor — vulgar jokes about the body.

ex: Regulating the growth of large companies when they begin to become monopolistic is a difficult task for government in a capitalist county; if it limits monopolies too much, the nation’s firms could become less competitive than foreign companies that enjoy the advantages [[accruing]] from greater monopolies.
mn: Like interest that ACCRUES steadily in a bank account.

d: to correct by punishment or reproof; to restrain or subdue
plain: to discipline or subdue through correction
ex: The child’s behavior improved after she had been [[chastened]] by punishment.
mn: CHASTEN sounds like 'chastise' — to correct someone through punishment or reproof.

ex: The student approaches her studies with commendable [[sobriety]].

ex: In his novel The Mayor of Casterbridge, Thomas Hardy describes an ancient Roman amphitheater where lovers often arranged secret [[trysts]].
mn: Tryst sounds like 'trust' between lovers meeting in secret.

d: to give up a position, right, or power
plain: formally give up power or position
ex: Romulus Augustus, the last Western Roman emperor, was forced to [[abdicate]] the throne in 476 A.D., and the Germanic chieftain Odovacar became the de facto ruler of Italy.
mn: Ab- (away) + dicate (declare) = to declare oneself away from power.

ex: The young man was [[discomfited]] being the only male in the play.
mn: Discomfit sounds like 'discomfort' -- to cause unease or embarrassment.
trap: related to but stronger than 'discomfort' the noun; means to confuse/disconcert

ex: Geologists measure the width of the [[fissure]] regularly to monitor movement of the Earth’s plates in the area.
mn: Fissure shares roots with 'fission' — a split or crack.

ex: The judge cautioned the attorney to present only information that was [[substantive]] to the case at hand.
mn: Substantive = has 'substance' — real and meaningful.

d: a branch of philosophy that investigates the ultimate nature of reality
ex: To skeptics, [[metaphysics]] is an arbitrary search for a chimerical truth.
mn: Meta (beyond) + physics = beyond the physical — study of ultimate reality.

d: formation or use of words that imitate sounds of the actions they refer to
ex: One theory of the origin of language is that it began as a sort of [[onomatopoeia]] as early humans imitated sounds they heard.
mn: Words like 'buzz' or 'hiss' that sound like what they mean.

ex: The scientist Carl Sagan wrote about astronomy and other scientific subjects in a way that enabled a reader with even a [[modicum]] of knowledge of science to understand what he was saying.
mn: Modicum ~ 'moderate' amount — just a small dose.

ex: The American psychiatrist Frank Pittman said, “Men who have been raised violently have every reason to believe it is appropriate for them to control others through violence; they feel no [[compunction]] over being violent to women, children, and one another.”
mn: Compunction ~ a 'puncture' of conscience — a prick of guilt.

ex: Wilfred Owens’s famous poem “Dulce Et Decorum Est” describes an unfortunate soldier who was unable to get his gas mask on in time, seen through the [[stygian]] gloom of poison gas:
mn: From the River Styx in the underworld — hellishly dark.

ex: Instead of [[grousing]] about the policy, do something about it: write to your congressional representative.
mn: Sounds grumpy like the bird's name — 'grouse' = to grumble.

d: concerning the sky or heavens; sublime
ex: Astronomers make use of the Doppler effect to measure the velocities and distance from Earth of stars and other [[celestial]] objects.
mn: Celestial ~ related to 'celeste' (sky) — of the heavens.

plain: mutually destructive, esp. within a group
ex: The U.S. Civil War (1861-1865) was an [[internecine]] conflict that lead to the deaths of 620,000 soldiers out of the 2.4 million who fought in the war.
mn: Internal + 'necine' (killing) — deadly conflict within one group.

plain: a feeling something will happen; forewarning
ex: Shortly after his reelection in 1864, President Abraham Lincoln had a [[premonition]] of his impending death, and on April 14, 1865, he was shot and died the next day.
mn: Pre- (before) + monition (warning, as in 'admonish') = warning beforehand.

ex: It has been argued that the emphasis on so-called “proper English” leads to unnatural and [[affected]] speech.
mn: 'Affected' = acting unnaturally, putting on airs.

ex: To relax in the evening the judge likes to watch [[vapid]] situation comedies on TV.
mn: Sounds like 'vapor' — all the flavor evaporated, leaving it flat.

d: to dull the senses of; stun; astonish
plain: to shock or numb the mind
ex: After drinking three glasses of wine, Linda was [[stupefied]].
mn: Stupefy ~ 'stupid' — stunned into a dazed, stupid-seeming state.

ex: The professor’s editor advised him to change his writing style so that it was less pedantic and [[turgid]] if he wanted to appeal to a mass audience.
mn: Like 'turgor' (plant-cell swelling) — physically swollen or swollen with big words.

ex: The defendant [[quailed]] when the judge entered the room to announce the sentence.
mn: Like the skittish quail bird — flees at the first sign of danger.

ex: The poet William Blake believed that each person creates “mind-forged manacles,” [[fettering]] his or her natural instincts and spirit.
mn: Fetters are chains around the feet, restraining movement.

ex: Scientists have found chimpanzees to be a territorial species; individuals that are not members of a group [[impinging]] on the territory of that group are normally met with aggression.
mn: Think of 'pinning' against or striking upon someone's territory.

d: number of members necessary to conduct a meeting
ex: The U.S. Senate’s majority leader asked three members of his party to be available to help form a [[quorum]].
mn: Sounds like 'core-um' — the core number needed to proceed.

ex: To say that Napoleon Bonaparte achieved what he did merely because he was compensating for his shortness is simplistic, reductionistic, and [[implausible]].
mn: Im- (not) + plausible — not believable.

ex: The literature exam requires students to [[explicate]] three poems they studied in class and one they have not studied.
mn: Explicate ~ make 'explicit' — spell something out clearly.

d: sentimental longing for a past time
ex: The product’s marketing is centered on [[nostalgia]] for the 1950s.
mn: Greek 'nostos' (return home) + 'algia' (pain) — the pain of missing home/the past.

ex: The judge told the convicted man that he would come to [[rue]] his decision to commit the crime.
mn: Rue sounds like 'ruin' — you regret it because it ruined things.

d: excessively ornate; highly decorated; style of architecture in eighteenth-century Europe
ex: In music, the [[Rococo]] period (1730-1780) comes between the preceding Baroque period and the subsequent Classical period. The highly ornamented style of the Rococo period created new forms of dissonance that to listeners in previous eras would have sounded cacophonous.
mn: Rococo sounds as fancy and curly as its swirling decorative style.

ex: The boy’s father worried that his disobedient and [[petulant]] child would grow up to be a bitter and annoying man.
mn: Think of a spoiled 'pet' throwing a petulant tantrum.

ex: None of the dictator’s [[servile]] citizens dared question his decree.
mn: Servile ~ 'servant' — acting like a slavish servant.

ex: Minority members of the committee [[remonstrated]] with the majority members, saying that the proposal was unjust; nevertheless, it was approved.
mn: Sounds like arguing to 'demonstrate against' a decision.

ex: The businessman’s biography tells how he went from being an [[impecunious]] student in the 1980s to one of the richest people in America.
mn: Im- (not) + pecunious (money-related, as in 'pecuniary') = moneyless.

ex: Some people have the ability to prosper and live happily despite life’s inevitable [[vexations]].
mn: Vexation is the state of being 'vexed' — irritated.

d: to make an attempt; subject to a test
ex: The composer began work on a sonata, a form she had not previously [[essayed]].
mn: As a verb, to 'essay' something means to attempt it.

ex: The encyclopedia editors worked hard to cut out [[extraneous]] material so that readers could find information easily on a given subject.
mn: Extraneous ~ 'extra' — stuff that isn't needed.

plain: a feature that adds comfort or convenience
ex: Many [[amenities]] considered normal and necessary by people in developed countries, such as indoor plumbing, were luxuries only a few generations ago.
mn: Amenity ~ 'amiable' — pleasant features that add comfort.

ex: The Nobel Prize-winning scientist attributed his success to what he termed “curiosity, a modicum of intelligence, and [[sedulous]] application.”
mn: Think 'steady' + 'zealous' — steadily zealous in effort.

ex: The teacher had no choice but to send the [[froward]] child to the vice-principal for disciplining.
mn: Froward = turned 'from' what's wanted — the opposite of 'toward', i.e. contrary.

ex: [[Demographic]] trends in many European countries indicate that in the next generation there will be relatively fewer working people to support retired people.
mn: Demo- (people, as in 'democracy') + graphic (data) = data about people.

ex: Dan became so proficient at his [[avocation]] —computer programming—that he is thinking of giving up his job as a teacher to do it full time.
mn: Vocation is your job; avocation is away (a-) from it — a hobby.

ex: Modern technology is so complex and [[multifarious]] that it requires thousands of specialists to devise and operate; thus, even a brilliant engineer could not by himself fabricate a sophisticated radio or computer without the help of existing black boxes and expertise.
mn: Multi- (many) + farious (varied forms) = having many different forms.

d: based on the attitude that one’s group is superior
plain: believing one's own group is superior
ex: The words “primitive” and “savage” reflect an [[ethnocentric]] bias in Western culture that regards societies that do not have Western science and technology as inferior because they have not achieved as much material success as Western societies.
mn: Ethno (ethnic group) + centric (centered) = centered on one's own group as superior.

d: to insert; change by adding new words or material
plain: to insert new material into a text
ex: The book The Five Gospels was produced by having leading Bible scholars vote on which sayings of Jesus they believe to be authentic and which they believe to have been [[interpolated]] by other writers.
mn: Inter- (between) — inserting new words between existing ones.

d: dissection, surgery, or painful experiments performed on a living animal for the purpose of scientific research
plain: surgery or experiments on live animals
ex: The book Animal Rights by the philosopher Tom Regan contains a long discussion of [[vivisection]].
mn: Vivi- (alive, as in 'vivid') + section (cutting) = cutting into a living being.

ex: The Monica Lewinsky scandal, which led to President Bill Clinton’s impeachment in 1998, must certainly rank as one of the most [[sordid]] affairs in American history.
mn: Sounds like 'so dirty' — filthy and morally low.

ex: The prisoner was [[emaciated]] after being fed only bread and water for three months.
mn: From Latin 'macer' (thin) — wasted away to thinness.

ex: According to the chivalric code, a knight was never supposed to be [[churlish]], especially toward noble ladies, to whom he was supposed to be unfailingly gentle and courteous.
mn: From 'churl', an old word for a rude peasant — behaving like a boor.

d: a person who does all sorts of work; a handyman
plain: a person who does all kinds of work
ex: In Shakespeare’s play Twelfth Night, the character Malvolio aspires to become more than merely a [[factotum]] in the house of Lady Olivia.
mn: Latin 'fac totum' = 'do everything.'

plain: able to perceive and feel; conscious
ex: Charles Darwin regarded many animals as being [[sentient]] and as having intelligence.
mn: Sentient ~ 'sense' — able to sense and feel.

ex: In Jane Austen’s novel Pride and Prejudice, the youngest of the five Bennett daughters, Lydia, is portrayed as a [[vacuous]] young woman with few interests other than having fun.
mn: Vacuous ~ 'vacuum' — an empty space, empty-headed.

ex: Alistair Cooke’s book Six Men contains character studies of [[estimable]] modern figures including H. L. Mencken, Humphrey Bogart, and Adlai Stevenson.
mn: Estimable ~ 'esteem' — worthy of esteem.

d: characteristic of the countryside; rustic; pastoral
ex: The south end of Toronto’s beautiful High Park is a [[bucolic]] expanse of land that is perfect for anyone wanting a quiet walk.
mn: From Greek 'boukolos' (cowherd) — peaceful, cattle-grazing countryside.

d: a creature that is half-man, half-beast with the horns and legs of a goat; it is a follower of Dionysos; a lecher
ex: One of the best-known [[satyrs]] is Pan, the god of the woods in Greek mythology.
mn: A goat-legged mythical follower of Dionysus, known for lechery — not to be confused with 'satire.'

ex: The depressing though inescapable conclusion the journalist reached is that the mayor went into politics for motives that were almost entirely [[venal]].
mn: Venal ~ 'vend' — will sell their principles for money.

d: science of classification; in biology, the process of classifying organisms in categories
ex: In the late seventeenth century and the eighteenth century accurate observation of organisms developed, leading to the development of the sciences of [[taxonomy]] and morphology (the study of the form and structure of organisms.)
mn: From Greek 'taxis' (order) + '-nomy' (study) — the study of ordering things.

ex: Former U.S. presidents Lyndon Johnson, Ronald Reagan, and Bill Clinton often [[regaled]] visitors with amusing political anecdotes.
mn: Sounds like 'royal' — entertained like royalty with feasts and tales.

plain: to renounce or give up formally
ex: Most members of the Religious Society of Friends (commonly known as the Quakers or Friends) [[abjure]] the use of violence to settle disputes between nations.
mn: Ab- (away) + jure (swear) = swear away from — formally renounce.

ex: Lawyers are sometimes [[maligned]] as greedy and dishonest.
mn: Malign ~ 'mal' (bad) — saying bad things about someone.

ex: The [[sodden]] field makes it difficult for the soccer players to move effectively.
mn: Left sodden by a sudden downpour.

ex: When the long list of casualties from the battle were announced, the mood in the room was [[saturnine]].
mn: From the planet Saturn, astrologically linked to a cold, sluggish, gloomy temperament.

d: practice widely observed in a group; custom; accepted technique or device
plain: a widely accepted custom or rule
ex: The critic praised the novel for defying literary [[convention]].
mn: 'Conventional' behavior — the usual accepted way of doing things.

ex: The 80-year-old actor came out of retirement to give a [[valedictory]] performance on Broadway.
mn: A 'valedictorian' gives the farewell speech at graduation.

plain: marked by short, abrupt, clear-cut sounds
ex: We listened to the [[staccato]] steps of the woman in high heels running down the street.
mn: A musical term for short, detached, abrupt notes.

d: to stop or check the flow of
plain: to stop or check the flow of
ex: The country’s government has put controls on currency movement to [[stanch]] the flow of money out of the country.
mn: Staunchly stopping the bleeding or the flow.

ex: Despite widespread opposition to his plan, the party’s leader is [[adamant]] that it must move to the center to appeal to moderate voters.
mn: Relates to 'diamond' (hardest stone) — an unbreakably firm stance.

d: funeral ceremony (often used in the plural, obsequies)
ex: Solemn [[obsequies]] were held for President John F. Kennedy following his assassination on November 22, 1963.
mn: Sounds like 'obsequious' but means funeral rites, final respects paid.

ex: The general’s words were spoken in the [[peremptory]] tone of a man who is used to having his commands obeyed without question.
mn: An order so final there's no room for discussion.

ex: One theory of the evolution of high intelligence in primates is that it evolved largely as a result of [[Machiavellian]] calculations on the part of apes.
mn: Named after Machiavelli's The Prince — the ends justify the means.

ex: The [[brazen]] student irritated his teacher by saying that he could learn more from a day spent “surfing” the World Wide Web than a day spent in school.
mn: Brazen ~ 'brass' — brass-faced, bold and shameless.

ex: What is considered [[gauche]] in one culture might not be considered gauche in another culture; for example, burping is considered rude in America but is acceptable in China.
mn: French for 'left' — the left hand was historically seen as clumsy.

ex: Don Juan is a legendary, archetypal [[libertine]] whose story has been told by many poets, such as Lord Byron.
mn: Liberty taken too far — total freedom from moral restraint.

ex: The Treaty of Versailles, which concluded World War I, was deliberately [[vindictive]], imposing tremendous penalties on the defeated nation.
mn: Vindictive ~ 'vindicate' taken too far — vengefully trying to get even.

d: group of people united in political intrigue
plain: a group ruling after seizing political power
ex: The country’s ruling [[junta]] consists of a general, an admiral, and the mayor of the capital city.
mn: Spanish for 'joined' — a small group that seizes power, often via coup.

d: song of joy or triumph; a fervent expression of joy
plain: a song or expression of joy/triumph
ex: Fundamentally, the poem is a [[paean]] of joy, celebrating the coming of democracy to the country.
mn: Sounds like a 'payment' of praise — a joyful tribute.

ex: The questioning of scientific and religious orthodoxy by scientists such as Charles Lyell and Charles Darwin led to stupendous advances in both geology and biology, as these fields freed themselves from the fetters of [[hallowed]], but fallacious, assumptions about the age and development of the Earth and life.
mn: As in 'All Hallows' Eve' (Halloween) — hallowed means holy.

ex: The discovery of the bones of a person with the [[appellation]] Kennewick Man in the state of Washington in 1996 has raised important questions about who the earliest people to populate America were.
mn: Appellation ~ what someone is 'called.'

plain: a brief feeling of hurt pride/resentment
ex: Sally left the restaurant in a fit of [[pique]] after her date called to say he couldn’t come because he was working late.
mn: Pride 'peaks' then stings when hurt — 'a fit of pique.'

plain: the state of no longer being used
ex: NASA is considering a plan to refurbish booster rockets from the Apollo Program that have fallen into [[desuetude]].
mn: De- (away) + suetude (custom, related to 'habit') — fallen away from use.

ex: The CIA gathers information about foreign intelligence through many means, including [[covert]] ones.
mn: Covert ~ 'cover' — kept covered, hidden.

d: calm and peaceful; happy; golden; prosperous
plain: calm and peaceful, esp. of the past; golden
ex: The movie evokes the [[halcyon]] years immediately after World War II when America was at peace and the economy was booming.
mn: From a Greek myth bird that calmed the sea to nest — peaceful, golden days.

plain: a beggar, esp. a religious one
ex: In Thailand it is traditional for young men to become monks for a year, a period during which they become [[mendicants]].
mn: One who has to 'mend' a life of poverty by begging.

ex: The sociologist theorizes that what may seem like [[prattle]] often has an important social function: what might be labeled “gossip” is an important means for people to communicate valuable information about themselves and others.
mn: Sounds like a baby's babble — meaningless chatter.

ex: The writer [[cloistered]] herself in a country house to finish her novel.
mn: Like monks secluded in monastery cloisters.

ex: Over the past 12 years or so the voices [[clamoring]] for better protection of the Earth’s rain forests have increased dramatically.
mn: A noisy 'claim' or demand made publicly.

d: medication that reduces or eliminates pain
ex: Aspirin (the trademark of the drug acetylsalicylic acid) is a powerful [[analgesic]] that was introduced in 1899 and is still one of the most effective medicines available to alleviate pain, fever, and inflammation.
mn: An- (without) + algesic (pain, as in 'neuralgia') = without pain.

ex: The public execution of [[miscreants]] was common in Great Britain in the eighteenth century.
mn: Mis- (wrong) + creant (believing, as in 'creed') — originally 'unbeliever', now a villain.

ex: Speed walking, cross-country running, and marathons are normally regarded as [[adjuncts]] of track and field athletics since races in these sports are not normally held on a track.
mn: Ad- (to) + junct (joined, as in 'junction') — joined on to the main thing.

d: existing in a wild or untamed state
plain: wild, having reverted to an untamed state
ex: [[Feral]] dogs returning to an untamed state after domestication sometimes form packs, becoming a threat to humans.
mn: From Latin 'fera' (wild beast) — untamed.

plain: to make amends for, atone for
ex: The pilgrims undertook their long journey to [[expiate]] their sins.
mn: Ex- (out) + piate (pious) — paying out through pious acts to atone.

d: so excessive as to be disgusting
ex: The actor was embarrassed by the [[fulsome]] praise he received after winning the Academy Award for best actor.
mn: So 'full' of praise it becomes sickening and insincere.

ex: Humans are at the acme of their [[linguistic]] proficiency in the first several years of life, during which they master thousands of complex grammatical operations.
mn: From Latin 'lingua' (tongue/language).

plain: letting light through but not clear
ex: The architect decided to install a [[translucent]] door in the room to allow outside light to shine in.
mn: Trans- (through) + lucent (light, as in 'lucid') = light passes through.

ex: Hosts of television talk shows are generally people who possess a great deal of [[geniality]].
mn: Geniality ~ 'genial' — a warm, friendly nature.

d: relating to a herbivore, an animal that feeds mainly on plants
ex: Most researchers now believe that the common ancestor of apes and humans was a strongly [[herbivorous]] animal.
mn: Herbi- (plant) + vorous (eating, as in 'devour') = plant-eating.

d: medicine or remedy of doubtful effectiveness; supposed cure
ex: Although there are many [[nostrums]] urged on obese consumers, the only effective remedy for this condition is prosaic but nonetheless valid: eat less and exercise more.
mn: Latin 'nostrum' = 'our own' — the quack's 'own' secret cure.

d: touching; neighboring; connecting without a break
plain: adjoining, touching, next to each other
ex: There are 48 [[contiguous]] states in the United States of America.
mn: Con- (together) + tig (touch, as in 'tangible') — touching together.

ex: Every year the Edinburgh Festival in Scotland gives [[thespians]] from around the world the opportunity to perform before a diverse audience.
mn: Named after Thespis, the first recorded Greek actor.

ex: The head coach warned her players not to [[vaunt]] their undefeated record.
mn: Sounds like 'vanity' — vainly boasting.

plain: a marsh; a difficult, complicated situation
ex: The federal government’s antitrust suit in the 1990s against Microsoft created a legal [[quagmire]].
mn: 'Quag' (bog) + 'mire' (mud) — stuck in mud, literally or figuratively.

ex: On the queen’s neck was a necklace of jewels, in the middle of which was a large, [[refulgent]] diamond.
mn: Re- + fulgent (shining, as in 'effulgent') — shining brightly.

d: to win over by flattery or coaxing
plain: to persuade through trickery or flattery
ex: The students [[inveigled]] their professor into postponing the test for a week.
mn: Sounds like veiling true intent while sweet-talking someone.

d: to feign illness to escape duty
plain: to feign illness to avoid work
ex: In order to discourage [[malingering]], the company decided to require employees taking sick leave to produce a doctor’s certification of their illness.
mn: Mal- (bad) + linger — badly lingering, dodging duty by faking sickness.

d: likely to provoke ill will; offensive
plain: offensively unfair, likely to provoke resentment
ex: Most publications in the United States prohibit their writers from making [[invidious]] comparisons between racial groups.
mn: From Latin 'invidia' (envy) — causing envy or resentment.

d: the power to entice by charm
plain: the power to entice by charm
ex: Political groups in the United States often lobby Congress to use the [[allure]] of America’s vast market as an incentive for countries to pursue policies in accordance with American policies.
mn: Allure ~ 'lure' — something that lures you in with charm.

ex: An enduring image of the Great Depression in America is the out-of-work man [[cadging]] money with the line, “Hey, mister, can you spare a dime for a cup of coffee?”
mn: Picture someone scrounging for scraps, cadging a coin.

ex: The English poet William Blake believed his work [[presaged]] a new age in which people would achieve political, social, psychological, and spiritual freedom.
mn: Pre- (before) + sage (wise) — a wise sign that comes before an event.

d: article treating a subject systematically and thoroughly
plain: a formal, detailed written work on a subject
ex: The thesis of the philosopher’s [[treatise]] is that reality is, ultimately, opaque to human understanding.
mn: A treatise 'treats' a subject thoroughly in writing.

ex: John tried to hide his [[trepidation]] when he proposed to Susie, the girl he loved.
mn: Trepidation is the fear that the 'intrepid' (fearless) lack.

ex: Some people have called the philosopher Freidrich Nietzsche a [[misogynist]] because of the numerous negative comments he made about women.
mn: Miso- (hatred, as in 'misanthrope') + gyn (woman, as in 'gynecology') = hatred of women.

d: something that completes or makes up a whole
plain: something that completes or perfects another
ex: Some people envision chess developing into a game played at the highest levels between teams of humans and computers, each [[complementing]] the other and providing investigators with insight into the cognitive processes of each.
mn: Complement has an 'e' like 'complete' — it completes something.

ex: Bankruptcy laws should not be too stringent, or not enough people will venture their capital; on the other hand, they should not be too [[liberal]], or entrepreneurs will take unreasonable risks and waste capital.
mn: From 'liberty' — giving freedom, or resources, generously.

ex: In the late eighteenth century, Great Britain tried unsuccessfully to put down the uprising against their rule by [[contumacious]] Americans, leading eventually to the establishment of a separate nation.
mn: Contempt + audacious — showing contemptuous defiance of authority.

ex: The mayor resorted to behind-the-scenes [[machinations]] to try to win his party’s nomination for governor.
mn: Like gears of a 'machine' working behind the scenes.

ex: Unless the phrase “repeat again” is being used to refer to something that has occurred more than twice, it is a [[tautology]].
mn: Greek 'tauto' (same) + 'logos' (word) — saying the same thing twice.

plain: to place side by side for comparison
ex: To illustrate their case, opponents of functionalism [[juxtapose]] the products of modern architecture and those of classical architecture, such as the Parthenon, or those of medieval architecture, such as the Cathedral of Notre-Dame.
mn: Juxta- (near) + pose (place) = place near each other.

plain: to complain about petty things, find fault
ex: Reviewers were [[carping]] about minor typos while ignoring the novel's strengths.
mn: A carp is a bottom-feeding fish — carping is nagging, petty fault-finding.

ex: Most attempts to create advanced new technology by government fiat [[founder]], probably because of the difficulty in anticipating changes in the fluid world of high technology.
mn: A ship taking on water sinks to the seabed — founders.

d: not to be avoided or escaped; inevitable
ex: No one can escape the [[ineluctable]] truth that every creature that is born will one day die.
mn: In- (not) + eluctable (from 'elude') = cannot be eluded.

ex: The judge said she would not sentence the man to jail on the condition that he pay full [[reparation]] to the family hurt by his crime.
mn: Reparation ~ 'repair' — repairing damage through compensation.

d: to go back on one’s word
ex: Generally, if one party to an agreement [[reneges]] on its contractual obligations, it must provide appropriate compensation to the other party.
mn: Re- + negate — negating an earlier promise.

ex: The playwright complained that the musical comedy version of his play was a [[travesty]] of his work.
mn: An adaptation so wrong it mocks the original.

plain: to systematize, arrange into a formal system
ex: The state legislature voted to [[codify]] regulations governing banking fraud.
mn: Codify ~ turn into a 'code' — an organized system of rules.

plain: a person's face or facial expression
ex: The infant studied its mother’s [[visage]] intently.
mn: Visage ~ 'vis-' (see, as in 'vision') — what you see: the face.

ex: Many people in the nineteenth century denied the evolutionary significance of the [[simian]] characteristics of human beings.
mn: From Latin 'simia' (ape).

d: the act of cutting; the natural separation of a leaf or other part of a plant
plain: the act of cutting off; natural separation
ex: Two scientists, Alan G. Williams and Thomas G. Whitham, have hypothesized that premature leaf [[abscission]] is an adaptive plant response to herbivorous attack.
mn: Ab- (away) + scission (cutting, as in 'scissors') = cutting away.

ex: The school board decided that the book is too [[salacious]] to be in the school library.
mn: Think 'saucy' talk — sexually charged content.

d: a form of deductive reasoning that has a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion
plain: a deductive argument: two premises, one conclusion
ex: The following [[syllogism]] is often taught in logic courses: “All Xs are Ys, all Ys are Zs; therefore, all Xs are Zs.”
mn: Syn- (together) + logos (reason) — reasoning together to a conclusion.

plain: to skip and jump playfully, frolic
ex: The children [[gamboled]] on the lawn while their parents ate lunch.
mn: Picture lambs gamboling playfully in a field.

ex: Improvements in antivirus software have [[allayed]] many people’s fears of having their computers “infected” with malicious software.
mn: Allay ~ 'lay' your fears to rest.

ex: Archeological evidence indicates that women have been using makeup to give color to a [[pallid]] face for millennia.
mn: Pallid ~ 'pale' — sickly pale.

ex: The prose of writers discussing lofty subjects sometimes becomes [[tumid]].
mn: Tumid ~ 'tumor' — swollen, or writing swollen with big words.

d: bored because of frequent indulgence; unconcerned
ex: We were amazed by John’s [[blasé]] attitude toward school; he seems to have made it a rule never to open a book.
mn: French for so used to luxury/excitement that nothing excites anymore.

ex: The ancient Greeks believed that [[overweening]] pride—what they called hubris—would be punished, eventually, by the gods.
mn: Over- + weening (thinking, old English) — thinking far too much of oneself.

ex: Microbiologists study [[Lilliputian]] organisms.
mn: From Gulliver's Travels, the tiny people of Lilliput.

ex: Many of us have in our mind the stereotype of the [[cantankerous]] old man who is constantly complaining about something or other.
mn: A grumpy, hard-to-please, cantankerous old-timer.

ex: Gradually what had been a [[platonic]] relationship between Tim and Kyoko became a romantic one.
mn: Named after Plato, who valued spiritual love over the physical.

plain: the underlying reason or justification for something
ex: The philosophy of “enlightened self-interest” justifies acting in one’s own interest by asserting that this is not selfish or motivated by a “beggar thy neighbor” [[rationale]], but is simply the best way to ensure the welfare of the entire community.
mn: Rationale ~ 'rational' — the rational basis behind a decision.

plain: to depict or portray in words/art
ex: The artist based his painting on a sketch he had [[limned]] several years earlier.
mn: Sounds like sketching the 'limbs'/outline of a figure.

ex: In World War II, many soldiers went to war with [[diaphanous]] dreams of glory, but found instead horror and death.
mn: Dia- (through) + phan (show, as in 'phantom') — light shows through, sheer fabric.

d: using or containing harsh, abusive censure
ex: The young music critic’s [[vituperative]] comments aroused the wrath of nearly every serious composer.
mn: Words sharp enough to puncture and wound viciously.

ex: [[Concave]] lenses are used in glasses to compensate for myopia (nearsightedness).
mn: Concave ~ curves inward like the inside of a cave.

plain: a smaller group within a larger organization
ex: The workers formed an informal [[caucus]] to discuss their difficulties.
mn: A core group that meets to decide policy or candidates.

d: many colored; made up of many parts
plain: made up of very different elements, many-colored
ex: The new political party is made up of a [[motley]] group of people who are unhappy with the existing parties.
mn: As in a 'motley crew' — a colorful, mismatched group.

d: a variety of animals kept together
plain: a diverse collection of animals kept together
ex: Linda seems to take home every abandoned pet in the town; she now has an incredible [[menagerie]] of dogs, cats, turtles, rabbits, and other animals.
mn: A menagerie is a managed collection of animals.

ex: The main character in the novel returns home safely after his [[sundry]] adventures.
mn: As in 'all and sundry' — items of every different sort.

plain: rising and falling smoothly like waves
ex: The [[undulating]] terrain of the area has made it difficult for engineers to build roads there.
mn: From Latin 'unda' (wave) — moving in a wave-like pattern.

ex: Despite the salesperson’s [[blandishments]], Donna did not buy the car.
mn: Bland-sounding sweet talk used to coax someone.

plain: to increase in power, status, or size
ex: One of the concerns of the framers of the U.S. Constitution was that one branch of government would try to [[aggrandize]] itself at the expense of the others.
mn: Aggrandize ~ 'grand' — making something grander than it truly is.

ex: The philosopher Plato believed there is a [[causal]] relationship between income inequality, on the one hand, and political discontent and crime, on the other hand: in his Laws he quantified his argument, contending that the income of the rich should be no more than five times that of the poor, and he proposed policies to limit extremes of wealth and poverty.
mn: Causal ~ 'cause' — describes a cause-and-effect link.

ex: At first, the Native Americans were not too concerned about the [[incursions]] of European settlers, but their anxiety grew with the relentless flow of people, until, finally, calamitous wars were fought between the two sides.
mn: In- + cursion (running, as in 'cursor') — running in suddenly to attack.

plain: to ask or raise doubt about
ex: Until widespread industrialization caused massive pollution in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the ability of the biosphere to dissipate and assimilate waste created by human activity was not [[queried]].
mn: Like a database 'query' — asking for information.

plain: a long, repetitive recitation or list
ex: The student listened intently to his teacher’s [[litany]] of the grammatical errors committed by the class.
mn: From church litanies — long, repeated prayers, now any long repetitive list.

d: related to the woods or forest
ex: The house’s [[sylvan]] setting provides the family with beauty and tranquility.
mn: From Latin 'silva' (forest) — think 'Pennsylvania', Penn's Woods.

ex: John Steinbeck’s novel The Grapes of Wrath portrays the [[abject]] poverty of many people during the Great Depression.
mn: Ab- (away) + ject (thrown) — thrown down into misery.

d: point in an orbit that is closest to the Earth
plain: the point in an orbit closest to Earth
ex: The Earth observation satellite reaches a [[perigee]] of 320 miles above the Earth’s surface.
mn: Peri- (near) + gee (Earth, as in 'geo') — near Earth.

d: relating to practices connected with supernatural phenomena
ex: In his book Supernature the biologist Lyell Watson explores what he regards as phenomena on the border between natural and [[occult]] phenomena.
mn: Occult ~ hidden, mysterious, supernatural knowledge.

plain: irritable and difficult to control, unruly
ex: In an effort to unify their divided party, its leaders decided to first placate the party’s most [[fractious]] elements.
mn: Relationships with this person easily 'fracture.'

d: to sanctify; to bless; to ascribe a virtue to
plain: to declare holy or blessed, sanctify
ex: In the year 2000 Pope John Paul II traveled to Fatima in Portugal to [[beatify]] two of the three children who said they saw the appearance of the Virgin Mary there in 1917.
mn: Beat- (blessed, as in 'beatitude') + '-ify' — to make blessed.

ex: The historian has a knack for focusing on information that appears [[nugatory]] but that, upon examination, illuminates the central issue.
mn: Sounds like a golden 'nugget' but ironically means worthless, like fool's gold.

ex: Traditionally, a ship captain is considered [[pusillanimous]] if he abandons his ship before everyone else has.
mn: Latin 'pusillus' (tiny) + 'animus' (spirit) — a tiny spirit, cowardly.

ex: The Sophists often gave interminable speeches full of rhetorical [[flourishes]].
mn: Flourish ~ 'flower' — adding decorative flowery touches.

ex: At the bottom of the [[limpid]] pond we could see hundreds of fish swimming.
mn: Water so calm and clear it barely seems to move.

d: a violent upheaval that causes great destruction and change
plain: a sudden violent disaster or upheaval
ex: The French Revolution of 1789 was a [[cataclysm]] whose effects are still felt today.
mn: Cata- (down) + clysm (a great wash, as in 'deluge') — a devastating upheaval.

ex: Most of our knowledge of [[antediluvian]] times has been built up as a result of one of humanity’s grandest collaborative endeavors—the gathering, identification, dating, and categorization of fossils as they are discovered.
mn: Ante- (before) + diluvian (flood, as in 'deluge') = before Noah's flood.

ex: In his book Poetic Meter and Poetic Form, the literary citric Paul Fussell quotes this bit of [[doggerel]] from a U.S. Army latrine during World War II:
mn: Verse that's gone to the dogs — low quality.

d: expecting an improvement; favorable to health
plain: producing a beneficial or healthy effect
ex: The system of universal education is in our age the most prominent and [[salutary]] feature of the spirit of enlightenment...”
mn: Salutary ~ a 'salute' to health — beneficial to well-being.

d: sheer; light and delicate, like cobwebs
ex: Some experts in NASA believe that what they call a gigantic “ [[gossamer]] spacecraft” could be constructed in space using extremely lightweight materials.
mn: Like fine spider-web threads — delicate and light.

ex: In Greek mythology, the god Zeus often appeared to mortal women to whom he was attracted in strange [[guises]]: as a swan, he made love to Leda of Sparta, with other women he took on the form of a shower of gold, or a bull, or thunder and lightning.
mn: Guise sounds like 'disguise' minus the 'dis' — an appearance, often false.

d: use of obstructive tactics in a legislature to block passage of a law
plain: the use of obstructive tactics to block legislation
ex: The senator threatened that his [[filibuster]] would include a full reading of his eight-volume autobiography.
mn: Sounds like 'fill-a-buster' — filling time to bust/block a vote.

d: to relate to a particular cause or source; attribute the fault to; assign as a characteristic
plain: to attribute (fault or quality) to someone
ex: Primatologists generally [[impute]] relatively high intelligence to chimpanzees based on, among other things, the ability of chimpanzees to recognize themselves in a mirror.
mn: In- + pute (reckon, as in 'compute') — reckoning something as belonging to someone.

plain: lasting only a short time, temporary
ex: A hypothesis to explain the fact that American states in which the population is composed of a large number of recently settled people (California, for example) tend to have high rates of crime, suicide, divorce, and other social problems is that anomie is higher in [[transient]] populations than in more stable populations, resulting in more antisocial behavior.
mn: Transient ~ 'transit' — just passing through.

d: mixture of writings on various subjects
plain: a mixed collection, esp. of writings
ex: The book is a fascinating [[miscellany]] collected from the writer’s life work.
mn: Miscellany ~ 'miscellaneous' — a mixed bag of writings.

d: a small system having analogies to a larger system; small world
plain: a small system representing a larger one
ex: For many years the atom was seen as a sort of [[microcosm]] of the larger universe, with electrons—analogous to the planets of a solar system—orbiting the nucleus, or “sun.”
mn: Micro- (small) + cosm (world, as in 'cosmos') = a small world reflecting the big one.

ex: The police were called in to break up a [[fracas]] that had erupted in the bar.
mn: Sounds like 'fracture' — a brawl that can fracture things.

ex: Bob tends to nick himself when he shaves, so he uses an [[astringent]] aftershave to stop the bleeding.
mn: Astringent lotion tightens skin; figuratively, astringent words sting.

plain: a merging or blending into one
ex: A hydrogen bomb requires tremendous heat to trigger the [[fusion]] reaction, which is provided by the detonation of a fission bomb.
mn: Fusion ~ 'fuse together' — merging into one, as in nuclear fusion.

d: to speak or write at length
plain: to speak or write about something in detail
ex: Every year the book club invites a famous author to come to [[expatiate]] on the art of writing.
mn: Ex- (out) + spatiate (space, as in 'spatial') — spreading out at length.

ex: When folk artists such as Bob Dylan began to use rock instruments, many folk music traditionalists considered it an [[execrable]] travesty.
mn: From 'execrate' (to curse) — so bad it deserves to be cursed.

d: one who asks humbly and earnestly
plain: one who asks or begs humbly and earnestly
ex: The mother of the man sentenced to be executed appeared as a [[supplicant]] before the governor, asking him to grant her son clemency.
mn: Supplicant ~ 'supplicate' (to beg humbly).

ex: The journey “inward” to explore the unconscious mind has been described as more [[harrowing]] than the most dangerous voyage to explore the Earth.
mn: A harrow tears up soil; a harrowing experience tears you up emotionally.

ex: The politician’s speech is filled with [[emollient]] phrases to make his message more palatable.
mn: Like a soothing skin cream — figuratively, soothing words.

plain: to take the place of, replace
ex: The “Frankenstein monster” fear of some people is that AI machines will eventually [[supplant]] biological life forms, making such life redundant or even subservient.
mn: Sup- + plant — planting yourself in someone else's place.

ex: The family lives in [[squalor]] in the slums of Mexico City.
mn: Squalor ~ 'squalid' — filthy, degraded conditions.

plain: a rule or principle guiding conduct
ex: A good [[precept]] to follow in writing is to avoid redundancies such as “track record” (unless the record was set on a racecourse), “revert back,” “free gift,” and “general consensus.”
mn: Pre- + cept (take, as in 'concept') — a rule taken up beforehand to guide conduct.

d: study of past geological eras through fossil remains
plain: the study of ancient life through fossils
ex: By analyzing fossilized bones, researchers in [[paleontology]] reconstructed the dinosaur's likely gait.
mn: Paleo- (ancient) + ontology (study of being) = study of ancient life via fossils.

d: tending to call to mind or produce a reaction
plain: strongly suggestive, bringing something to mind
ex: Somerset Maugham’s short stories are often [[evocative]] of exotic places such as Pago-Pago and Gibraltar.
mn: Evocative ~ 'evoke' — calls to mind images or feelings.

d: person compulsorily enrolled for military service
ex: The position of NOW (The National Organization for Women) is that having male-only [[conscripts]] violates the principle of gender equality.
mn: Con- + script (write, enroll) — enrolled by force onto a list.

plain: superficially attractive but insincere or false
ex: One of the allures of jargon is that it can make a poor idea appear worthwhile, or something [[meretricious]] easier to accept because it is dressed in fancy language.
mn: From Latin 'meretrix' — flashy, cheap, insincere allure.

ex: Successful investment bankers are sometimes accused of [[avarice]]; their defenders, however, say that they are simply very good at what they do and should be rewarded accordingly.
mn: Avarice ~ an insatiable desire to be 'a-very-rich.'

d: prolonged feud marked by bitter hostility
plain: a long-running, bitter feud or revenge campaign
ex: The judge warned both families that the [[vendetta]] between them had to end at once.
mn: Italian, related to 'vengeance' — a blood feud.

d: the giving up of certain pleasures
ex: The monk’s vow of [[abstinence]] includes all intoxicating substances.
mn: Abstinence ~ to 'abstain' — holding oneself back from something.

ex: It took two hours for the princess’ handmaidens to help her put on her splendid [[raiment]] for her coronation as queen.
mn: An old word for 'garment' — clothing.

ex: The critic [[lambasted]] the movie in her column, calling it “the most insipid, jejune film made in our generation.”
mn: 'Lamb' + 'baste' — basting (beating) someone verbally like meat.

ex: A Chinese proverb describes a paradox: Rich [[spendthrifts]] never save enough; but the poor always manage to save something.
mn: Ironic: a spendthrift spends instead of being thrifty.

ex: The court ruled that the movie could be censored because its sole aim was to promote [[lascivious]] thoughts.
mn: Lascivious sounds as sleazy as its meaning — driven by lust.

ex: One of the jobs of an ambassador is to provide a [[convivial]] atmosphere for diplomats to meet.
mn: Con- (together) + viv (live, as in 'vivid') — living it up together, festive company.

plain: an obsession with one's own power or importance
ex: In his farewell speech the retiring trial judge warned his colleagues to beware of [[megalomania]] as they exercise their power in the courtroom.
mn: Megalo- (great) + mania (obsession) = obsession with one's own greatness.

ex: The United States is generally considered to be a secular society in which church and state are separate; however, religion plays a large role, since nearly everyone [[purports]] to believe in God and many people are members of churches.
mn: Pur- + port (carry) — carrying forward a claim, whether true or not.

ex: The governor engaged in some [[banter]] with reporters before getting to the serious business of the news conference.
mn: Light, back-and-forth teasing chat.

d: to forbid; prohibit; to confront and halt the activities, advance, or entry of
ex: Under U.S. law, [[interdicted]] goods can be seized by customs officials.
mn: Inter- (between) + dict (decree) — a decree placed between someone and an action.

d: the characteristic quality of sound produced by a particular instrument or voice; tone color
plain: the distinctive tone quality of a sound
ex: The audience was delighted by the rich [[timbre]] of the singer’s soprano.
mn: Sounds like 'timber' (wood) but refers to the unique color of a sound.
